### 4.10 Chapter 14: the subjection of creation

**Where.** A new section after "Real, but not ultimate" (L17). About 600 words. Units: F01, F03–F07, F09, F11, C09, C12, C13, F08. Depends on decisions 6, 10, 11. A reminder of Ch4's two constraint levels is required (recall distance: ten chapters).

> ## The subjection of creation
>
> Scripture traces the disorder of the world to an event. After the man and the woman had eaten, God's word reached past them into the ground itself:
>
> > `And unto Adam he said, Because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife, and hast eaten of the tree, of which I commanded thee, saying, Thou shalt not eat of it: cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life; Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field; In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.`
> > *Genesis 3:17-19*
>
> Three things need to be kept apart.
>
> *What the text says.* The ground is cursed because of human disobedience. Work becomes toil, the earth yields thorns, and the man will return to dust. Paul adds that the creation "was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who hath subjected the same in hope" (Romans 8:20). The subjection is God's act.
>
> *The author's interpretation.* The curse is a deliberate divine realignment of created runtime order to the consequences of spiritual disobedience. Its purpose is that creation should go on telling the truth. A world in which the breach between humanity and God had no visible consequence would teach falsely about what had happened. On this reading creation remains an instructor after the Fall, and what it now teaches includes decay, toil and loss. **Status:** theological interpretation. Genesis does not describe a mechanism, and the interpretation does not claim that it does.
>
> *The mechanism, which is open.* The author's thesis is that God realigned the primitives themselves, the explicitly intrinsic constraints of Chapter 4. Two other readings belong in view. God may have changed settings within a primitive order that stayed fixed. Or he may have brought about a new state of creation under its original constraints, so that the new conditions follow as implicitly intrinsic constraints. These are different claims, and they would explain different things. Appendix E records them as a research question.
>
> One consequence holds on every reading. The subjection of creation is God's act, and God's acts are not corrupt. Corruption, as the next section describes it, is parasitic: a distortion with no being of its own. The futility to which creation was subjected is a judgement, coherent and purposed, and given "in hope". Corruption suffered in the higher orders of creation does not mean that its primitive order has become incoherent.
>
> Nor does every suffering follow from the sufferer's own sin. Asked whose sin had made a man blind, Jesus answered:
>
> > `Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him.`
> > *John 9:3*
>
> Creation's subjection is the condition of all. It is not a ledger of each.

Decision 11 adds one sentence on non-human death, either way.

## Deviations from the Phase A plan

- **Order of work.** Editorial cuts were made chapter by chapter, immediately before each chapter's additions, not in one pass across the book first. "Delete before elaborating" held within each chapter, and each chapter was read once instead of twice.
- **Shorter drafts.** Chapters 12–16 were drafted more tightly than the plan's prose because of the reading budget.
- **Q3(b).** The author chose the stronger grounding objection. The Chapter 3 paragraph states it as internally contradictory under the book's grounding requirement, and expressly not as a claim about mathematical infinities.
- **Q6(b).** Making the *that* of B a premise excluded A and C at premise level. Chapter 3, Chapter 9 and App E.9 were reworded accordingly, beyond the plan's §4.7.
- **Q11.** The author chose post-Fall animal mortality. The resulting fossil-record interface was put to the author (option 1: state, name the conflict, do not resolve).

  <rect x="140" y="220" width="1320" height="1950" rx="24" fill="#0c0e14" fill-opacity="0.84"/><text x="800.0" y="330" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="56" fill="#efe6d2" font-weight="bold" font-style="normal" text-anchor="middle" letter-spacing="6">COHERENT BIBLICAL ONTOLOGY</text><text x="800.0" y="398" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="40" fill="#d6b875" font-weight="normal" font-style="italic" text-anchor="middle" letter-spacing="0">Second Edition, revision 2.7</text><text x="215" y="560" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="38" fill="#ebe2cd" font-weight="normal" font-style="normal" text-anchor="start" letter-spacing="0">Physics predicts with astonishing precision. It does</text><text x="215" y="622" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="38" fill="#ebe2cd" font-weight="normal" font-style="normal" text-anchor="start" letter-spacing="0">not thereby tell us what kind of created reality lets</text><text x="215" y="684" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="38" fill="#ebe2cd" font-weight="normal" font-style="normal" text-anchor="start" letter-spacing="0">physical order, life, persons, moral consequence and</text><text x="215" y="746" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="38" fill="#ebe2cd" font-weight="normal" font-style="normal" text-anchor="start" letter-spacing="0">Scripture belong coherently to one world. This book asks.</text><text x="215" y="848" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="38" fill="#ebe2cd" font-weight="normal" font-style="normal" text-anchor="start" letter-spacing="0">Its answer is that created physical reality is relational</text><text x="215" y="910" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="38" fill="#ebe2cd" font-weight="normal" font-style="normal" text-anchor="start" letter-spacing="0">from its foundation, which is why independently located</text><text x="215" y="972" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="38" fill="#ebe2cd" font-weight="normal" font-style="normal" text-anchor="start" letter-spacing="0">things everywhere share one grammar of interaction. What</text><text x="215" y="1034" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="38" fill="#ebe2cd" font-weight="normal" font-style="normal" text-anchor="start" letter-spacing="0">happens is drawn by constrained chance from what created</text><text x="215" y="1096" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="38" fill="#ebe2cd" font-weight="normal" font-style="normal" text-anchor="start" letter-spacing="0">order makes possible, and it carries its history into</text><text x="215" y="1158" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="38" fill="#ebe2cd" font-weight="normal" font-style="normal" text-anchor="start" letter-spacing="0">the present. A distinction becomes consequential through</text><text x="215" y="1220" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="38" fill="#ebe2cd" font-weight="normal" font-style="normal" text-anchor="start" letter-spacing="0">one recurring grammar: transmit, carry, receive.</text><text x="215" y="1322" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="38" fill="#ebe2cd" font-weight="normal" font-style="normal" text-anchor="start" letter-spacing="0">Because the material world is relational at its base,</text><text x="215" y="1384" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="38" fill="#ebe2cd" font-weight="normal" font-style="normal" text-anchor="start" letter-spacing="0">promise, responsibility and love are not bolted onto an</text><text x="215" y="1446" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="38" fill="#ebe2cd" font-weight="normal" font-style="normal" text-anchor="start" letter-spacing="0">alien world. Yet material, living, personal and spiritual</text><text x="215" y="1508" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="38" fill="#ebe2cd" font-weight="normal" font-style="normal" text-anchor="start" letter-spacing="0">realities remain distinct, and creation is not God.</text><text x="215" y="1610" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="38" fill="#ebe2cd" font-weight="normal" font-style="normal" text-anchor="start" letter-spacing="0">The argument is one of global coherence, constrained by</text><text x="215" y="1672" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="38" fill="#ebe2cd" font-weight="normal" font-style="normal" text-anchor="start" letter-spacing="0">observation, governed by Scripture, and stated clearly</text><text x="215" y="1734" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="38" fill="#ebe2cd" font-weight="normal" font-style="normal" text-anchor="start" letter-spacing="0">enough to be wrong. An appendix sets out the book's</text><text x="215" y="1796" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="38" fill="#ebe2cd" font-weight="normal" font-style="normal" text-anchor="start" letter-spacing="0">current ontology, claim by claim.</text><line x1="560" y1="1898" x2="1040" y2="1898" stroke="#d6b875" stroke-width="2"/><text x="800.0" y="1978" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="32" fill="#c9bfa8" font-weight="normal" font-style="normal" text-anchor="middle" letter-spacing="0">A free electronic edition and the full research record:</text><text x="800.0" y="2030" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="34" fill="#e8d6a6" font-weight="normal" font-style="normal" text-anchor="middle" letter-spacing="0">relational-substrate.blogspot.com</text><text x="800.0" y="2078" font-family="DejaVu Serif, Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-size="34" fill="#e8d6a6" font-weight="normal" font-style="normal" text-anchor="middle" letter-spacing="0">github.com/gellsmore-svg/Relational-Substrate</text>
</svg>

# Coherent Biblical Ontology

## Second Edition

*A Scripture-first account of a relational creation: how physical order, life, persons, corruption and restoration belong to one world without collapsing into one kind of thing.*

Second edition, revision 2.7, October 2026. Companion volumes: *The Relational Substrate* (technical), *A Coherent World* (general), *How to Hug the Right Tree* (devotional).

---

# Preface

A discipline can be exact in its own domain and still leave the deepest questions about reality unanswered. Physics is the clearest case. It predicts with astonishing precision, and nothing in this book disputes that. But a theory can predict well without telling us why its entities are compatible with one another at all, why the same grammar of interaction holds in every place we look, why the world is mathematically describable, how living things and persons belong to the same order, or why the weight of a promise or a betrayal is not alien to the stuff of which bodies are made. These are not questions physics has failed at. They are questions its success leaves open.

This book exists to ask them together. Its question is not whether modern science works. It does. The question is what kind of created reality can make everything we know, physical, living, personal, moral and revealed, belong coherently to one world.

The book's answer is that created physical reality is *relational* from its foundation. Things are not first made as sealed, self-contained objects that are later connected. They are constituted within an order of relation that God made and upholds. The project calls that order the Relational Substrate. Matter, on this proposal, is fully real but not foundational. That it derives from a foundation that is not itself material is held as a theological premise, and the book's central question is how materiality, the acquisition of persistent, manipulable individuality, arises within such an order. Two further proposals give the answer its working shape:

- what actually happens is drawn, with real chance, from what the created order makes possible and favours;
- a difference anywhere becomes consequential somewhere else through one recurring grammar: something distinguishes, the distinction is carried by a dependency that preserves it, and another state is changed because of it.

The book calls that grammar transmit, carry, receive, and comes to treat it as a candidate form of consequential relation itself.

Scripture governs the whole. The book begins where the Bible begins, with God creating a world that is really there, and it lets the biblical distinctions between Creator and creature, dust and breath, body and person, corruption and restoration set boundaries the ontology must respect. A relation-first world does not turn morality into physics or persons into patterns. It does mean that the moral and personal life Scripture describes is not bolted onto a world that has no room for it.

## How the argument is judged

The standard is *global coherence*. A proposal about what exists must hold together across every domain it touches. It must not change the meaning of its terms as it crosses from physics to life to persons. It must not need unexplained interfaces where one kind of reality meets another. It must not break one domain to fix another. That standard runs in both directions. The book must not contradict what has been observed and measured, or what successful mathematics predicts. Equally, the picture of reality commonly carried along with physics, a world of independent objects in a container of space, is itself a proposal and is tested in the same way. Observation and measurement constrain every ontology. Familiarity, consensus and habit constrain none.

The book makes several kinds of claim and labels them. Some things are stated because Scripture states them. Some are observed and measured. Some are inferences. Some are working hypotheses of this project, and some questions are simply open. Chapter 2 sets out these levels. Appendix E gathers the book's current ontology in one place, with the status of each claim. A reader who rejects one claim can see exactly which others depend on it.

No set of measurements could display the deepest structure of created reality directly, so the book's warrant for the Relational Substrate is that of a global coherence argument, not of experiment. It states a hypothesis clearly enough to be wrong, shows why it is believed, shows what supports it and what would count against it, and follows its consequences to the end. The way of reasoning it uses, inference that tests itself against the whole and revises itself where it fails, is part of what it offers.

## About this edition

The book is written for an intelligent reader with no specialist training in physics, philosophy or theology who is willing to think carefully. Each technical term is explained where it is first needed. The opening chapter introduces one ordinary scene, seeing a stone in daylight, which returns throughout as a common reference point.

This is revision 2.7 of the second edition. The first edition rested on specific mechanisms that later work did not support. The second rebuilds the book on more foundational ideas, and Appendix B records what changed and why. The research behind the book is the work of one author, carried out with extensive computational and AI-assisted exploration. Its records are public, and Appendix B notes what they do and do not show.

A free electronic edition of this book is available, offered as an open intellectual contribution to encourage reading, sharing and honest discussion. Updated versions and related materials can be found through the project website at <https://relational-substrate.blogspot.com/> and the public research repository at <https://github.com/gellsmore-svg/Relational-Substrate>.

# Chapter 1: Scripture and the World That Is There

Begin with something ordinary. It is a clear morning, and a stone lies on the path in front of you. You see its grey surface, a vein of lighter mineral, the shadow it casts. You could pick it up, feel its weight, put it in your pocket, and find it there tomorrow, still the same stone.

Nothing could be more familiar, and almost nothing about it is simple. What is the stone, at the deepest level we can reach? What is the light that brings it to you, and how does that light become your seeing? Why is it the same stone tomorrow, when much about it and about you will have changed? Why does light behave so regularly that we can calculate exactly how it will bend through glass? And who is the one who sees, recognises, names and decides to pick it up?

The stone will return many times in what follows. It was chosen because every idea the book needs is present in the scene, not because the scene proves anything. Before any of those questions can be asked well, though, a prior decision has to be made: where does the inquiry begin?

## Scripture speaks first

This book begins with Scripture. That is a decision with consequences, and it should be made openly.

> `All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works.`
> *2 Timothy 3:16-17*

Scripture claims its own authority, and this book receives that claim. Scripture is authoritative in the form it actually takes. Genesis is narrative, theological and liturgical, not a laboratory report, and it is not a hidden vocabulary for physics. Scripture does not overstep its own truthfulness. Human interpretation can overstep, on both sides. When the Bible and a scientific account seem to collide, the fault almost always lies in a human extension: a reading pressed beyond what the text says, or a metaphysical conclusion drawn beyond what the measurements show. It does not lie in revelation, or in careful measurement as such.

What Scripture-first does mean is this: Scripture sets the boundaries within which an account of reality may be built. It tells us what kind of world exists, who made it, what has gone wrong with it, and what God is doing about it. Inside those boundaries there is room for patient inquiry into how the world works. A proposal that contradicts what Scripture teaches about creation is ruled out, however elegant it is. A proposal that Scripture neither teaches nor forbids may be explored, but it must never be presented as though the Bible taught it.

That last point will govern the whole book. The Relational Substrate is a modern proposal. Scripture never mentions it. So the book keeps four relations between Scripture and its proposal carefully apart:

- *Scripture teaches* something: the world is created, held, good, and distinct from God.
- The proposal *is consistent with* what Scripture teaches.
- The proposal offers *a possible mechanism compatible with* a scriptural claim, without Scripture teaching the mechanism.
- Scripture *provokes a question* that the proposal explores.

The first sets real boundaries. The others never borrow its authority.

## A world that is really there

Genesis does not begin with an idea, a possibility or a meditation. It begins with an act.

> `In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.`
> `And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters.`
> `And God said, Let there be light: and there was light.`
> *Genesis 1:1-3*

The order of the verses matters. The heaven and the earth are created in the first verse. In the second, the earth is already there, though unformed and empty. The deep is there. The waters are there. Darkness is upon the face of the deep. Only then is light spoken into being. Genesis 1:1 is therefore best read as a real beginning, the creation of a world that exists. What follows is formation, separation, filling and manifestation *within* that world, not the gradual appearance of reality out of nothing.

This has a quiet but important consequence for the darkness of verse 2. In ordinary speech, darkness can mean the mere absence of light, or something threatening, or moral evil. Later Scripture uses darkness in all those senses, and rightly. But in Genesis 1:2 darkness belongs to created reality before light is spoken. The text says only that darkness was upon the face of the deep, and that light then came. Two things are plain in the text: the darkness of verse 2 is not nothing, since the earth, the deep and the waters are already there with it, and it is not presented as evil. From the sequence the book draws an inference, and labels it as one: darkness here is a real condition of a real world, not yet manifest in the visible order that follows. Scripture elsewhere speaks of darkness as having its own created place:

> `Where is the way where light dwelleth? and as for darkness, where is the place thereof.`
> *Job 38:19*

This matters for everything that follows. If darkness were nothing, then light would be the arrival of existence itself, and whatever cannot be seen would seem less real than what can. Genesis forbids that. Visibility is not the measure of reality. The New Testament says the same thing directly:

> `Through faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear.`
> *Hebrews 11:3*

The visible world rests on what does not appear. That sentence will matter again when we ask what the stone is made of. Our instruments meet the world through its effects. Whatever is deepest in created order is likely to be known indirectly, through what it does, rather than displayed as one more visible object.

## The Creator and the creature

The second thing Scripture establishes is the most important boundary in the book. God made the world, and the world is not God.

> `Know ye that the LORD he is God: it is he that hath made us, and not we ourselves; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.`
> *Psalm 100:3*

> `Who changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen.`
> *Romans 1:25*

The distinction cuts both ways. Created things are not divine, so nothing in creation, however vast, orderly or mysterious, may be treated as God or as part of God. And created things are not self-explaining, so nothing in creation exists by its own power or holds itself together by its own right. It is held:

> `For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him: And he is before all things, and by him all things consist.`
> *Colossians 1:16-17*

> `God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands… For in him we live, and move, and have our being.`
> *Acts 17:24, 28*

"By him all things consist" means that all things hold together in him. Creation is coherent because it is held. This does not mean God is a part of creation, or that creation is a part of God. It means creation's coherence is never self-generated. Whatever the deepest physical order turns out to be, it is upheld, moment by moment, by the One who made it.

This boundary will be tested later, because the Relational Substrate is proposed as the deepest created order of the physical world. A deepest created order can easily be mistaken for something more than created. It can be imagined as a cosmic mind, a world-soul, or a quiet substitute for God. Scripture closes that door before the proposal is even stated. The substrate, if it exists, is a creature. It is not divine essence, not a rival principle, not intelligent in itself, and not the source of its own order.

## Kinds of reality

Genesis does more than say that God made a world. It describes a world with distinct kinds of reality in it.

The opening chapter is marked by three uses of the Hebrew verb *bara*, "create", the verb used only with God as subject. It appears at the beginning of everything (Genesis 1:1). It appears again when animate creaturely life appears: "God created great whales, and every living creature that moveth" (Genesis 1:21). And it appears a third time, three times in one verse, when humanity is made:

> `So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.`
> *Genesis 1:27*

The book does not rest its argument on a single Hebrew word. But the pattern the text shows is clear. Creation is not one flat category in which everything is the same sort of thing at different sizes. There is the material world. There is living creaturely life. There is humanity, made in the image of God. Genesis 2 shows the inner structure of that last threshold:

> `And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.`
> *Genesis 2:7*

Dust, breath and living soul: a body formed from the same material as the rest of creation, life imparted by God, and a living person who is more than the dust and yet not separable from it in this life. Chapter 12 will return to this verse at length. For now the point is simpler. Scripture distinguishes kinds of reality, which the book will call **categories**. The material is one category. The living is another, built on the material but not reducible to it. The personal is another. The spiritual is another. And God is not a category within creation at all, but its Creator.

Categories matter because the argument of this book has a particular risk. It will claim that physical reality is relational at its foundation, and later that relation also runs through life, persons, morality and redemption. A careless reader, or a careless author, could slide from "relation appears everywhere" to "everything is the same kind of thing". That slide would be a serious error, and Scripture itself shows why.

## The same word is not the same thing

Consider light. In Genesis 1:3 God says, "Let there be light", and there is created light. In the Gospel of John, Christ says:

> `I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.`
> *John 8:12*

And John's first letter says:

> `This then is the message which we have heard of him, and declare unto you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.`
> *1 John 1:5*

The same word is used for created light, for Christ and for God. It would be absurd to conclude that God is made of the light of Genesis 1:3, or that Christ is a kind of radiation. Yet the word is not used by accident either. Created light discloses, makes visible, brings what was hidden into view, and allows sight. These are structural features, and they are shared by what Christ does in bringing truth, life and the knowledge of God. The physical and the spiritual share a *form* of relation: one thing making another manifest. They do not share a *nature*.

This is the distinction the whole book depends on, and it deserves a name. A **structural analogy** is a likeness of form between things of different kinds. **Ontological identity** would mean they are the same kind of thing. Scripture is full of structural analogies, such as light, bread, water, seed, word and body, and they are real. Creation was made by the Word, and it bears likenesses of its Maker and of the spiritual realities it serves. But likeness of form across categories never erases the categories. When this book later shows the same relational pattern in a beam of light, in a living cell, in a conversation and in the history of redemption, it will be pointing to analogies of form, not claiming that redemption is a physical process. The reader is entitled to hold the book to that promise.

Likeness of form is not the only way different kinds of reality are joined, though, and the book needs to say which joining it means. Four relations are kept apart. A **structural analogy** is a likeness of form between different kinds, as between created light and Christ's making-manifest. A **representation** is a created form that, by design, shows something of the spiritual order. Paul says that the invisible things of God "are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made" (Romans 1:20). That is more than resemblance: creation was made to disclose, and it instructs without being conscious of doing so. A **causal connection** holds within one human person, between an embodied act and its moral reality. A lie is spoken with a tongue, and it is also a wrong. The two are connected, and they are not the same thing. **Ontological identity**, sameness of kind across categories, the book rejects. Whenever a later chapter links one category to another, it says which of these it means.

## What Scripture leaves open, and what it rules out

Scripture's boundaries are real, and they exclude a good deal. If God created the world, the world is not eternal and did not make itself. If the world is not God, it is not divine in whole or in part. If creation is good, matter is not evil or illusory. If darkness is a created condition, it is not a co-eternal rival to light. Historically, each of these exclusions answers a serious position that thoughtful people have held. They are gathered in Appendix A for readers who want to see the points of divergence. The chapters that follow do not dwell on them, because their purpose is to build rather than to refute.

At the same time, Scripture leaves a great deal open. It does not tell us how electricity works, why the speed of light has the value it does, or what the deepest structure of matter is. It tells us the world is real, ordered, intelligible, dependent and good. It tells us the world is meant to be searched out:

> `It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter.`
> *Proverbs 25:2*

Some of Scripture's language provokes questions without answering them. The prophet speaks of the One

> `that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in.`
> *Isaiah 40:22*

Language like this sits uneasily with the habit of imagining space as an empty container that simply exists, and it invites the question of what extension itself is. It does not supply a geometry for the deep order of creation, and this book does not extract one from it. Scripture constrains and provokes.

Beginning here also gives inquiry its focus. An inquiry that treats every conceivable account of origins as equally likely has nowhere to start; beginning from one Creator and one created order narrows the field to what can actually be investigated.

## The questions the book will answer

Return to the stone on the path. Scripture has told us that the stone and the light and the one who sees them all belong to a real, created, ordered, dependent world. It has told us that the world is not God, that it holds together in Christ, and that its deepest order is not necessarily visible. It has told us that creation contains distinct kinds of reality, which may share forms of relation without sharing a nature.

That is the frame. It does not yet tell us what the stone is, how the light reaches us, or why the stone will still be a stone tomorrow. Those questions belong together, because the same world answers them all, and any account of the stone must also leave room for the one who sees it and for everything Scripture says about that person. To ask them well, one more thing is needed first. We need to be clear about the difference between describing how something behaves and knowing what it is, and about how human beings come to know anything at all when the deepest things cannot simply be seen. That is the work of the next chapter.

# Chapter 2: How We Come to Know What Is There

Suppose you drop the stone from the path. It falls. Time the fall and measure the height, and you can calculate how fast it struck the ground. With Newton's law you can calculate the orbit of the Moon, and with Einstein's general relativity the corrections that keep satellite navigation accurate to within metres. Physics knows how gravity behaves with extraordinary precision.

Now ask a different question. What *is* gravity? Is it a force reaching across space, as Newton's equations seem to say? Is it the curvature of a spacetime that exists as a kind of thing in its own right? Or is spacetime itself a set of relations between events, with no existence apart from them? Physicists and philosophers who accept every one of those measurements still disagree about these questions, and nobody yet knows how gravity fits with quantum theory. The disagreement is not about whether the stone falls, or how fast. It is about what kind of reality the equations describe.

That gap, between describing how something behaves and knowing what it is, is the subject of this chapter. Seeing it clearly is the key to everything this book attempts.

## Six layers of knowing

When we say we "know" something about the stone, we can mean several different things, and they must be kept apart.

1. We have **observed** it: seen it, touched it, noticed that it falls.
2. We have **measured** it, attaching numbers by a defined procedure: its mass, its temperature, the time of its fall.
3. We have found a **mathematical relation** that predicts the measurements, such as distance fallen growing with the square of the time.
4. We have a **physical model** that organises the behaviour, such as Earth's mass pulling on the stone's mass, or the stone following a straight path through curved spacetime.
5. We hold an **ontological interpretation** of the model: what must actually be there for the behaviour to happen at all.
6. We live within a **worldview** in which that interpretation feels natural.

Each layer depends on the ones before it, but the later layers are not guaranteed by the earlier ones. An equation can predict perfectly while different pictures of the mechanism remain possible. A mechanism can be useful while the question of what fundamentally exists remains open. The history of physics shows this repeatedly. Newton's law of gravitation predicted superbly for more than two centuries, yet the picture of a force acting instantly across empty space, which Newton himself found troubling, was eventually replaced by a very different picture in general relativity. The *predictions* were largely preserved, and many of them still underpin practical calculation today. The *account of what is there* changed profoundly.

Quantum theory makes the point sharper. Its mathematical machinery is among the most precisely confirmed in science. Yet the same mathematics is read in strikingly different ways. On some readings the world is fundamentally a matter of chance at the smallest scales. On others it is entirely deterministic, with hidden variables or branching worlds. These readings disagree about what reality is while agreeing about every measurement made so far. (A further family of theories modifies the quantum dynamics itself and predicts slight differences, which experiments are now testing.) A successful description can be joined to more than one ontology.

This is simply what descriptions are. A description tells us how things behave. An ontology asks what kind of thing has to be there for that behaviour to be possible. Confusing the layers causes trouble in both directions. When descriptive success is treated as though it had settled ontology, metaphysical assumptions enter unexamined. When the gap is used as an excuse to ignore description, the result is fantasy.

## What the outside of a thing can tell you

Computing offers an exact picture of the gap. Programmers often work with a *private function*: code they can call but cannot read. They supply an input and receive an output. By testing systematically they can learn a great deal: which outputs follow which inputs, which conditions change the behaviour, what the function refuses to do, and what stays the same whatever they try. That is real knowledge, and reliable software is built on it. What they cannot learn this way is how the function is written. Quite different code can give the same output for every input anyone has tried, and the function may do things nobody has yet asked of it.

So knowledge of **consequential behaviour**, meaning what something does and under what conditions, is genuine knowledge. It is not knowledge of **intrinsic ontology**, meaning what that something is, and the second does not follow automatically from the first. Mathematics has a precise case. In 1966 Mark Kac asked whether one can "hear the shape of a drum": whether the notes an ideal drumskin can sound fix its shape. Some things can be heard; the notes reveal the drum's area, for example. But in 1992 Carolyn Gordon, David Webb and Scott Wolpert produced two differently shaped drums that sound exactly the same notes. The sound tells you much about the drum, and not everything.

Observability and understanding answer different questions. Something may be observed without its mechanism being understood, or understood relationally without a complete mechanism. Four respects in which a question may stand need to be kept apart. **First, mechanistic explanation:** we can account for how specified relations and processes produce an outcome. **Second, relational understanding without a complete mechanism:** we may genuinely understand what trust is, or why a promise binds, without possessing an exhaustive account of how that reality operates. **Third, present investigative limits:** some questions lie beyond our available instruments, evidence or methods, yet may become accessible. **Fourth, possible limits of exhaustive creaturely comprehension:** some matters may never be comprehended in full by a creature, although genuine partial understanding remains possible. These are respects in which we approach questions, not four kinds of reality or permanent boxes.

Observability cuts across these respects. Atoms were inferred for generations before they could be imaged, and single atoms can now be seen and moved one at a time. Other things may be unobservable in principle: quantum theory limits what can be learned from a single unknown quantum system. Yet unobservability does not forbid inference from consequences. Two errors are to be avoided. One declares something permanently inaccessible without reason. The other assumes that every underlying reality will eventually be observed as one more object, and that assumption is itself a metaphysical claim. Creaturely knowledge, as Scripture describes it, is genuine and partial at once (Romans 1:20; 1 Corinthians 13:12), and Chapter 16 returns to that. The principle is this: **a successful description of observable consequences does not, by itself, establish the ultimate ontological nature of their cause.**

## Every account starts somewhere

If description does not settle ontology by itself, then every ontology contains something more than measurement. It contains assumptions about what kind of world could produce the measurements. That is true of materialist accounts, of religious accounts, and of the account in this book.

Here it helps to distinguish two things often run together. **Methodological naturalism** is a working rule of scientific practice: in the laboratory, explain natural phenomena by natural causes and test the explanations against observation. It is a sensible rule, and Christians practise it every day in chemistry, geology and medicine. **Metaphysical naturalism** is a claim about all of reality: nothing exists except the natural world that science studies. The second does not follow from the first. A method that looks only for natural causes cannot discover that nothing else exists, any more than a metal detector can discover that there is no wood. When the method is treated as though it had proved the metaphysics, an assumption has entered without being named.

The same discipline applies to theology. Quoting Scripture does not make an argument rigorous if the step from the text to the conclusion is left unexplained. This book begins from Scripture openly. It also tries to show, at each important point, whether a claim is something Scripture teaches, something inferred from what Scripture teaches, or a proposal that Scripture permits but does not state. Metaphysical honesty means making these assumptions and inferences visible, so a reader can see where they are and decide what to make of them.

## Explanations that bend to fit

Assumptions go wrong in one characteristic way, and it needs a name. Imagine someone who explains every odd event in a house, a creaking stair, a lost sock, a flickering light, by an invisible resident with no other specified properties. Each explanation is logically possible, and none can be refuted, because whenever the evidence changes the resident acquires whatever power the new evidence requires. Nothing it could meet would count against it, and so it explains nothing.

The book calls this **metaphysical elasticity**: assigning additional, insufficiently justified properties to an explanatory entity whenever they are needed to preserve an interpretation, without acknowledging the added assumptions or the evidence they would require. The author's informal name for it is the *Harry Potter problem*: in a world of spells, an unseen cause can be produced for anything.

Elasticity is not confined to ghosts. It occurs when a successful mathematical description is taken as evidence that its mathematical entities are fundamental substances, without that identification being argued separately. It occurs when a word is widened to rescue a thesis. If "matter" is stretched to cover whatever physics finds, then materialism can never be wrong, and it has stopped saying anything. And it could occur in this book. The relational substrate would become exactly such an invisible resident if it gained a new power for every new problem. The book's defence is to fix its commitments in advance (Appendix E), to say what would count against them (Chapter 9), and to price every addition. The rule binds the Relational Substrate as strictly as its rivals.

## The status of each claim

Because of that, the book keeps track of what kind of claim it is making. It does not label every sentence, which would make it unreadable, but it uses one small, fixed vocabulary of status throughout:

| Status | Example from this book |
| --- | --- |
| Scriptural or theological constraint | God created the heaven and the earth. The substrate, if it exists, is a creature (an inference from Scripture, marked as one). |
| Empirical observation | A dropped stone falls. |
| Mathematical or physical constraint | Distance fallen grows with the square of the time. General relativity's predictions are precisely confirmed. |
| Ontological inference | Description does not by itself settle ontology. |
| Relational Substrate working hypothesis | Physical things are constituted within relations. |
| Mechanism candidate | A specific proposed structure for matter. The book names such candidates and does not rely on them. |
| Open question | How consciousness relates to physical order. Whether quantum events are fundamentally chancy. |
| Rejected | That a coherent account is thereby true. |

Two further labels say where a claim came from, not how firmly it is held. A **model result** happened in one of the project's computer models, built on stated assumptions. A model can show that an idea is possible, coherent and capable of doing work. It cannot show that nature works that way. An **exploratory** result comes from research sessions not yet published as formal records. Appendix E gives the status of every major claim in the book.

## Local, regional and global coherence

How, then, does one judge an ontology, if no measurement can display it directly? The answer this book gives is **coherence**. Freedom from contradiction is necessary but not enough: an elaborate story can avoid every contradiction while remaining a set of tidy compartments, none really connected to the others. Coherence in this book's sense also asks whether the parts are connected, and whether real distinctions survive the connecting. It comes in three degrees of scope.

**Local coherence** is achieved when a model explains a bounded phenomenon internally. An equation fits the measurements of falling stones. A theory accounts for the colours of a particular kind of glass. A model reproduces a pattern in one regime. Much of science operates, quite properly, at this level.

**Regional coherence** is achieved when several neighbouring domains integrate. Chemistry turns out to be grounded in the physics of atoms. Molecular biology joins chemistry to the life of the cell. The physiology of the nerve joins the cell to the behaviour of the organism. Regional coherence is harder to win than local coherence, and more valuable, because each domain now checks the others.

**Global coherence** is achieved when the whole account of reality remains mutually compatible. That means physical observation and mathematics, the material and the living, consciousness and personhood, morality and meaning, history and lived experience, and, for a Christian account, theology and Scripture: creation, corruption, redemption and restoration. A globally coherent worldview does not need one set of assumptions for the laboratory, another for the courtroom, another for the hospital bedside and another for prayer.

![Figure 1. Three scopes of coherence, nested: local coherence (a model explains one bounded phenomenon), within regional coherence (neighbouring domains such as physics, chemistry and biology integrate), within global coherence (the whole account of reality, from physics to Scripture, remains mutually compatible).](v2/figures/fig-coherence.png)

What makes global coherence demanding is not only that nothing may contradict anything else. Several further tests matter, and they can be stated in ordinary terms.

- **Real connection.** The domains must be joined by intelligible transitions, not merely placed side by side. It is not enough that an account says true things about physics and true things about persons. It must be possible to see how the one bears on the other.
- **Valid interfaces.** Where one kind of reality meets another, as when a physical consequence becomes a biological signal or a capacity to act becomes a moral responsibility, the meeting must be explained, not assumed. An idea crossing a boundary must keep what is relevant and must not quietly turn into something of a different kind.
- **Meaning kept through the layers.** A claim carried through several explanatory levels should still be recognisably itself at the end. If a word like "identity" or "cause" changes meaning a little at each step, the account can sound plausible paragraph by paragraph and still fail as a whole.
- **Stability under repair.** Solving a problem in one domain must not break what already held together in another.
- **The round trip.** Take a claim from one domain through others and back again, for example from bodily identity to the identity of an organism to the identity of a person and back to the body. It should return substantially the same. Hidden drift shows up most clearly on the way home.
- **Accountable kinds of knowing.** Observation, measurement, mathematics, philosophical inference, personal encounter and revelation are different kinds of knowing. Each contributes to inference in its own way. They must be kept distinct, and none may silently overrule the others.

And through all of these, the real distinctions must survive: Creator and creature, the material and the spiritual, description and ontology, probability and arbitrariness, analogy and identity, what is possible and what is right, a person and a configuration. Connection is not reduction. An account that achieves smooth connection by erasing these is not more coherent. It has simply lost something real.

The book's central methodological thesis can now be stated. **Local explanatory success is not sufficient evidence that an ontology is true if that ontology produces contradiction elsewhere.** An account of physical reality may explain falling stones perfectly. If it also makes promises, responsibility or love unintelligible, so that they must be explained away as illusions, then it has a global problem that its local success cannot cure. Conversely, an account that coheres across all these domains, while respecting every robust observation, has a strong claim on our attention even if its deepest commitments cannot be measured directly.

This is a philosophical thesis, and Chapter 10 argues for it. Most working scientists are rightly occupied with local and regional coherence. Global coherence asks what their successes jointly require.

## Coherence runs both ways

The test applies in both directions. The Relational Substrate must not contradict what has been observed and measured, or what successful mathematics predicts. Any proposal that does is finished, however elegant it is.

But the picture of reality that commonly travels with physics is also a proposal. Space is a container. The world is a collection of independent objects. Fields and particles are the furniture of reality. Laws are rules things obey. These belong to layers four to six above, not to layers one to three. They are often well motivated, and some may be right. They gain no evidential weight from being familiar, mainstream, widely published or taught in every school. Consensus is a fact about people, not a measurement of the world. So the conventional metaphysics of physics is held to the same standard of global coherence as the proposal of this book, and it receives no exemption for being physics. That is a refusal to confuse what was measured with a picture of what was measured.

## Comparing without numbers

Judging between accounts needs one more tool. It corrects a common mistake, the assumption that unless a probability can be calculated, talk of likelihood is mere opinion. Three judgments are involved.

1. **Logical possibility.** An account contains no identified contradiction.
2. **Qualitative plausibility.** Given the relevant observations, constraints, assumptions and alternatives, one account is more or less plausible than another.
3. **Quantitative probability.** A number is assigned under a specified mathematical model.

The absence of the third does not invalidate the second. Suppose you must pass your hand along an electric fence twice, once a centimetre away and once a metre away, in comparable circumstances where a slip is possible. Contact is more likely on the first pass. Nobody needs a model of your breakfast, your sleep or every possible distraction to know this. Those things bear on both passes alike, and only the distance differs, so the ordering holds across every reasonable variation of them. What must stay explicit are the conditions it depends on: that the circumstances are comparable, and that contact is possible at all. **A justified qualitative ordering of likelihoods does not require an exhaustive quantitative model of reality.** Mathematicians have studied such orderings directly. Their theory of comparative probability shows that "more probable than" can be reasoned about rigorously without numbers, and that some perfectly consistent orderings cannot be turned into numbers at all.

So the book sorts its comparisons. A **robust** comparison survives every reasonable variation of its assumptions, as the fence comparison does. A **conditional** one holds only under assumptions that must be stated. Sometimes **no defensible ordering** is available, and then none is claimed. The converse mistake matters too: logical possibility carries no number, and an account is not improbable merely because it is complicated. Accounts are compared by what each assumes and what each leaves unexplained.

This gives coherence a sharper edge. **Global coherence concerns not only what is logically possible, but how naturally an account explains the observed relationships and regularities of created reality without unnecessary independent assumptions.** An account can be possible and still need a long run of unexplained coincidences. That it can be imagined does not make it comparatively plausible. Chapter 3 puts this to work.

## Human knowing is already like this

The appeal to coherence is not a special method invented for this book. It is how human beings come to know almost everything they know.

Consider a doctor diagnosing an illness. She has a set of symptoms, some test results and a patient's history, none of which is conclusive alone. She forms the diagnosis that best accounts for all of them together, and remains ready to revise it if a new result does not fit. A jury does the same with testimony and evidence. So does a historian reconstructing what happened in a century no living person saw. So, on a smaller scale, do you, when you recognise a friend's voice on a crackling telephone line. Philosophers call the pattern *inference to the best explanation*. **Human understanding normally depends on assembling the most coherent account available from incomplete evidence.** We rarely possess exhaustive, certain access to the facts. We judge, compare, anticipate and revise, and our comparisons are mostly qualitative, of exactly the kind just described.

If that is how ordinary knowing works, then asking for the most globally coherent account of reality is not an eccentric substitute for evidence. It is the same activity, carried out at the largest scale.

Behind this ordinary practice lies a distinction the book will need. **Logic** is the necessary structure of consistency, implication, exclusion and possibility. **Reasoning** is its application, which can be done well or badly. There is, first, the complete coherence of all that is, perfectly comprehended and perfectly applicable by the One who made it. The author calls this **true logic**. It belongs inseparably to God's own nature, and no creature possesses it exhaustively. And there is the way finite minds move toward it. The author's definition is exact: "Inferential logic is the recursive refinement of partial understanding towards true logic through the discovery and application of relational coherence within the boundaries of created runtime order." *Created runtime order* is the operating created world, which Chapter 3 describes. **Status:** theological premise (true logic); working definition (inferential logic).

Two words in that definition carry the weight. *Partial*: the doctor's diagnosis is genuine knowledge, and it is not everything. *Recursive*: a later finding can revise a conclusion, the assumptions behind it, and sometimes the question itself. Observation, measurement, experiment, mathematics, philosophical argument and the reading of Scripture are not routes running beside inference. They are what inference works with. And because revision can reach even the book's own foundational commitments, one distinction stays fixed: revising an account of coherence is never revising the coherence of what God has made.

## What observation decides, and what it cannot

Coherence is not truth. A worldview can be internally coherent and false; a detailed and consistent story about a flat Earth is still wrong. The book says this once, here, and takes it as read from now on. Observation constrains ontology powerfully, and in three ways.

Robust observation rules out accounts that contradict it, however elegant they are. It reveals regularities that any account must respect, even before it can explain them. And it tests specific proposals: several of the Relational Substrate project's have been tested, some survived, some failed, and the failures are recorded in the project's public research history.

What observation cannot do is display the deepest structure of created reality as one more visible object. It narrows the field and rarely, if ever, picks out a single winner. So the warrant this book offers for the Relational Substrate is not that of experiment. It is a **global coherence argument**, and it holds itself to a plain standard: what it proposes, why, what supports it, what would count against it, and what remains unknown. A hypothesis stated clearly enough to be wrong can be improved. One hedged until it says nothing cannot. Chapter 9 names observations that would count against particular claims.

What, then, is proof? In this book the word has a bounded sense. **Proof** is the achievement of enough warrant, under stated premises, scope and constraints, for an inferred relationship to be relied on in further reasoning: to become what the book calls a **coherence factor**. A mathematical proof has this character in its strongest form: within its axioms and rules its conclusion is settled. An experimental result has it within what its procedures can show. Philosophical and theological arguments have warrant of their own kinds. A coherence factor keeps its scope, its source, its uncertainties and its dependencies in view, so that it can be revised if later work requires. Proof in this sense is real, and it is never the possession of the whole truth of what it concerns. The aim of inquiry is accordingly **inferential precision**: discriminating well between candidate relationships, tracing the warrant for each, and keeping what remains uncertain open to correction.

The posture this asks for is what the first edition called *disciplined confidence*, and it cuts both ways. Confidence must not outrun its warrant. Nor should justified understanding be discounted because it falls short of exhaustive knowledge. Overclaiming and underclaiming are both failures of the same discipline.

With these tools in hand, the book can return to the stone and ask the first ontological question. The stone appears to be a separate thing, sitting on the path, distinct from the light, the air and you. Is that what it fundamentally is?

# Chapter 3: Relation Before Things

Look again at the stone and list what you know about it. It is grey. It is hard. It is heavy for its size. It is cold to the touch this morning. It has a definite shape, which casts a definite shadow.

Now notice something about each item on the list. Its greyness is how it answers daylight: which colours of light it returns and which it absorbs, as registered by an eye. In the dark it has no visible colour at all, though it remains disposed to answer light in that way. Its hardness is how it resists being pressed or scratched by other things. Its weight is the pull between it and the Earth; on the Moon the same stone would weigh about a sixth as much. Its coldness is the direction in which heat flows between it and your hand. Even its shape is the boundary at which it stops admitting things into its space and begins to resist them.

Every property on the list turns out to be a way the stone stands in relation to something else: light, pressure, the Earth, your hand, the region around it. Strip away all those relations and ask what is left. It is surprisingly hard to say.

This chapter asks whether that difficulty is telling us something about what the stone, and the physical world, fundamentally is.

## Two pictures of the world

There are two broad ways of picturing the physical world, and most people hold one of them without ever having chosen it.

On the first picture, reality is basically a collection of **separate objects**. Each object is complete in itself and possesses its own properties. The objects sit in an empty space that contains them and move through a time that flows independently of them. Relations between them, such as attraction, collision, causation or communication, are real enough, but they are secondary. They are added to objects that would exist just as they are without them. Think of billiard balls on a table: each ball is what it is, and the collisions happen to it from outside.

On the second picture, reality is fundamentally **relational**. Things are real and distinct, but they are constituted *within* relations rather than existing first and relating afterwards. What a thing is cannot be separated from how it stands to everything else. Space is an order of relations among things rather than an empty container waiting to be filled. Change is the reorganisation of relations rather than a sequence of objects being pushed around.

The first picture has been enormously useful, and in many practical situations it is perfectly adequate. Engineers build bridges with it. But it carries an assumption that is rarely stated: that the basic furniture of the world is mutually independent and self-contained, and that relation is an afterthought.

## What "material" means

Much of what follows turns on the word *material*, and it is easily stretched, so it needs a fixed meaning.

The stone is the paradigm. You can pick it up, carry it across the path and put it down, and it is the same stone in your hand as it was on the ground. The book takes that as its working definition. **A form of reality is material when it exhibits persistent, spatially individuated identity that can, in principle, be mechanically manipulated or relocated while preserving its continuity as an identifiable entity.** Hands are the reference point, and instruments extend them. A grain of sand under tweezers has been handled, and so has a single atom nudged across a surface by the tip of a microscope. Being too small or too far away to touch does not make something non-material.

The definition is deliberately narrower than "physical". A sound crossing a room is physical and consequential, but nobody can pick up a sound and carry it elsewhere. Chapter 6 develops that difference and the hard cases that test it. The definition is a working one, open to refinement. It is not to be widened whenever a case proves awkward, because a word that stretches to cover everything decides nothing.

## Why the object picture strains

There are reasons to doubt that assumption at the deepest level. Two come from physics, and one comes from coherence.

The first reason is that physics has found no truly isolated thing. Everything physics describes interacts, and its properties are specified by how it interacts. An electron's charge is not a little label it carries; it is its capacity to interact in a particular way. In quantum field theory, the mathematics treats particles as excitations of fields rather than as self-standing pellets in a void. What that mathematics describes is debated, but the pellet picture no longer sits comfortably at the base.

The second reason is that the deepest successful theories describe relations more naturally than things. General relativity describes gravity in terms of the geometry relating events. Quantum theory describes systems whose joint state cannot be broken down into separate states of the parts. This is entanglement, and it has been confirmed many times. Some have drawn relational conclusions: Leibniz, that space is nothing over and above the order of relations among things; Carlo Rovelli, that quantum properties are always relative to other systems; the structural realists, that our best theories most securely describe structure, the pattern of relations. These positions are contested, and the argument does not rest on any of them. They show that the same mathematics is compatible with relation-first readings. The description underdetermines the ontology.

The third reason comes from coherence rather than physics, and it matters most to this book. If the basic furniture of reality is self-contained objects, then causation, influence, communication, dependence, belonging and responsibility must each be added to a world that does not, in itself, contain any of them. That becomes a serious difficulty with life and persons, where relation is central, and Chapter 10 presses it.

## One grammar everywhere

There is a fact so ordinary that it is easy to miss. Pick up a piece of granite in Hampshire and another in Western Australia. They look alike, and that is not surprising: similar processes made them. The striking thing is something else. The two stones, formed half a world apart with no shared history that anyone arranged, are *mutually intelligible*. Bring them together and they press, scratch, warm and cool each other according to the same relations. Light from either is received by the same eye. A grain of one could be built into the crystal lattice of the other.

This holds everywhere. Independently located physical things can affect one another. Each has a receptivity compatible with what the other does. The same interaction relations hold in places that have never been in contact. Physical quantities are commensurable, so that the mass of a stone here and the mass of a star there are the same kind of thing. Matter everywhere composes into stable higher structures. Something newly encountered, a meteorite or a sample from another world, turns out to join the same causal grammar at once. So does something newly made: a new alloy or a newly synthesised molecule behaves coherently toward everything else, though no separate rule was ever written for it.

Call this **universal interoperability**. It is an observation, and an ontology has to account for it.

Part of it is less surprising than it looks. In any account where a composite's behaviour is built from the behaviour of its parts, new composites inherit their parts' compatibility. The deeper fact lies at the base. Every fundamental kind of thing shares one finely matched grammar. The electric charges of the proton and the electron, for example, are equal in size to at least one part in a thousand billion billion, which is why ordinary matter is neutral. Physicists do not treat this as luck. They look for a common structure that requires it, and have found partial ones.

An ontology of wholly self-contained objects cannot take it for free. If each thing is complete in itself, nothing in its own nature guarantees that it will have an interface compatible with every other thing. Something common must supply the interface. Serious accounts supply it in serious ways: common laws of nature, common fields, shared symmetries, common forms, universal dispositions, or a common generative history. Each of these does real work, and some come close to the view of this book. But each is a common structure doing exactly the work that the objects, taken as self-contained, could not do. The question to put to every ontology, this one included, is what that common structure is and what it costs.

A relation-first ontology answers directly. Things are constituted within one created relational order, so they inherit their compatibility from it. Interoperability is not a coincidence to be explained after the objects are in place. It is what being constituted within the same relations means. An object-first ontology has to recover that common grammar somewhere else.

The comparison is qualitative, in the sense of Chapter 2, and conditional. *If* each kind's capacities were specified independently of every other kind's, their exact matching would be a coincidence, and an account that needs such coincidences is less plausible than one that does not. No number can be put on this, because there is no defensible way to count the alternatives. None is needed for the ordering, provided the assumption it rests on is stated.

## Three propositions

The argument is sharper with the positions set side by side and the definition of *material* held fixed.

- **A. Material fundamentality.** Material entities are fundamental within creation. Their capacities to relate belong intrinsically to them, and material individuality does not arise from any more fundamental non-material created order.
- **B. A non-material foundation, with matter emergent.** A more fundamental created relational reality, not itself material, constitutes and sustains material individuality. Matter is genuinely real, but its materiality is emergent rather than self-standing.
- **C. Two fundamental orders.** Material entities and a distinct non-material relational order are both fundamental. The relational order supplies the capacities through which material entities interact, so their behaviour depends on it, but they are not constituted by it. This is the "non-material glue" view.

All three are compatible with the bare claim that the world was created: whichever is true was designed and is upheld by God, and design alone favours none of them. The author's theological premise goes further. *That* material existence derives from a foundation that is not itself material is held as a premise, in keeping with Hebrews 11:3's "things which are seen were not made of things which do appear" (Chapter 1). On that premise A and C are excluded. The comparison that follows is kept for two reasons: it reaches the same conclusion by a second, independent route, from what is observed, and it shows what B still owes.

**A** must give every fundamental kind of material thing intrinsic capacities that match every other kind's exactly. Pressed to explain the matching, it has three routes. It can say that a thing's capacities are intrinsically directed at its partners, so that a charge is, in its nature, a capacity to act on other charges. That is a serious position, and it is faithful to A, but it makes relation part of what things are. The disagreement with B then narrows to whether relational natures belong to separately fundamental things, or things to a relational order. It can add a governing order, laws or fields standing over the entities. That supplies the matching, but it is C without the name. Or it can say that the matching simply holds, which leaves it unexplained. None of this shows that A is incoherent. It shows that A, when pressed, relies on something it does not state.

A also meets pressure from physics. Material individuals are created and destroyed: radiation passing near an atomic nucleus can produce an electron and its antiparticle where there was no matter before. And particles of one kind carry no individual labels, so two electrons cannot be told apart even in principle. The natural response is that the fundamental things are not particles but fields. A field spread through all of space, however, is not a persistent, spatially individuated entity that can be picked up and moved. To call it material would keep the word and change the proposition, which is the elasticity Chapter 2 named.

**C** avoids A's difficulty by positing the relational order openly. Like B, it explains the matching by a common order. It pays with two fundamental orders instead of one, and it must still say why independently existing material entities fit that order so exactly. Until it does, part of the coincidence has only been moved.

**B** posits one order, and interoperability is what being constituted within it means. Its cost is different, and real. B owes an account of how stable material individuals arise within an order that is not itself material, and no such account has yet been demonstrated. The debt is one of mechanism: the premise says *that* matter is so founded, and *how* remains to be shown (Chapter 9).

The comparison is clear without being final. B does best on economy and on integration across domains, provided its debt can be paid. On this comparison alone, C remains open. A in its plain form carries the heaviest burden. One caution keeps this honest. B is a family, not only this book's view. A realist reading of quantum fields, on which particles are excitations of a field that is not itself a material object, belongs to it too. The considerations from physics favour the family. They do not single out its relational member, which has to be argued for on its own grounds.

## The claim: relation is foundational

The Relational Substrate project makes a definite proposal in response. It can be stated in one sentence. **What is most fundamental about created physical reality is relation.** Whatever appears as a stable, distinct unit, such as an atom, a stone or a star, appears as a configuration within relation, never as an item that first exists independently and then participates in relations secondarily.

In the terms just set out, this is Proposition B in its relational form. It is an **ontological thesis**, the book's central one. It is not an observation, since relation as such cannot be put on a laboratory bench, and it is not a theorem. It is a claim about what kind of reality best accounts for everything else we know. It is supported by the strain in the object picture, by the underdetermination of physical description and by universal interoperability. It would be weakened by an object-first account that explained interoperability, life and personhood with equal economy and fewer unexplained interfaces. The following chapters develop it and test it.

Three clarifications fix what *relation-first* means.

First, relation-first does not deny that things are real or distinct. The stone is really there, and it really is not the path. Distinctness is real. It is simply *derivative*: the stone's distinctness is carried by a stable pattern of relations, not by some separating gap between it and everything else. A knot in a rope is a useful picture here. The knot is real: it can be pointed to, counted and untied. Yet it is not a separate object added to the rope. It is a configuration of the rope itself. The picture breaks down in one place. A rope is made of fibres that exist before any knot is tied, whereas the relational proposal imagines no pre-existing material into which relations are then tied. The picture shows only how a real, distinct thing can be a configuration rather than an addition.

Second, relation in this sense is not a mental association. When we say two things are related, we sometimes mean only that someone thinks of them together. Here relation means a real standing-between in which each relatum is conditioned by the other, whether or not anyone is thinking about it. The Earth and the stone stand in such a relation whether or not anyone weighs the stone.

Third, relation-first is not the same as "everything interacts". Two things that are already fully what they are can interact without either one's identity depending on the interaction: two billiard balls collide and remain the same balls. That is *interactional* relation, and every ontology recognises it. The Relational Substrate proposal is stronger. It holds that physical things are *constituted* within relation, so that relation partly belongs to what they are, and is not only something that happens between them.

## The relational substrate

If relation is foundational, it is natural to ask what bears it. Relations of what, in what?

The project's answer is the **relational substrate**: the created relational order within which physical things are constituted and through which they act. The word *substrate* means "what lies beneath". It names the deepest created level of physical order: what must already be there for stable things, change, influence and persistence to be real.

The substrate is the deep order of this world, not a further thing behind it. It is not matter: matter, as Chapter 6 will argue, is a stable form *within* it. Nor is it a field of physics under another name, an ether filling empty space, or information detached from anything physical. A field is a mathematical representation, and the substrate is a proposal about the relational order such representations describe, not a rival to the mathematics. Three further points matter more.

- Whether it is spatial is open. Its structure might correspond closely to the space we experience; space might arise from an order that is not itself spatial; or the substrate might have adjacency and ordering from which measurable space emerges.
- It is not a mind. It thinks nothing and intends nothing.
- Above all, it is not God, and it is not a soul.

A language offers a comparison, with its limits. A word has its meaning only within the whole order of its language; torn out of it, it becomes a sound. The relational proposal says that physical things likewise have what they are within an order of relation. But a language is sustained by speakers who mean things by it, and the substrate has no speakers inside it. Its order is given by its Creator, not negotiated by its parts.

## Influence through continuity

One consequence follows directly. If relation is foundational, nothing acts on anything else across a gap of non-relation. Influence is always **mediated**: a consequence depends on a relation that connects it to its source. In the manifest world mediation often looks like something travelling. The stone affects your eye through light, the Earth affects the stone through gravitation, and your hand affects the stone through the contact of surfaces. But the claim is not about travel or distance. It is that no effect is produced across literally nothing.

Physics has moved in a consonant direction, away from instantaneous action at a distance and toward influences propagated at finite speed. The relational proposal goes deeper than any particular picture of propagation. Chapter 7 develops how a distinction becomes consequential to another state, which is the heart of mediated influence.

## Created order as operating

One more term is needed. The book speaks of **created runtime order**, borrowing a word from computing, where a program can be considered as written or as running. Creation can likewise be considered in its origin, the creative act by which it exists at all, or in its ongoing operation, the ordinary unfolding of physical process. *Runtime* names the second. The created runtime order is the operating, non-conscious created order that expresses itself materially. It is not everything that exists. God is not part of it, and souls and spiritual creatures, though created, are not members of it; what lies beyond it may lie beyond creaturely observation (Chapter 2). How the stone falls is a question about runtime order. Why there is a world in which stones fall is a question about creation. The borrowing has a sharp limit. Creation is not a computer, the world is not code, and God is not a programmer who wrote software and stepped away. A better image might be a piece of music, its composition distinguished from its performance, except that here the Composer also upholds every note as it sounds.

## What Scripture requires here

Scripture does not mention a relational substrate. What it does is set requirements that any account of the deep physical order must meet, and the relational proposal is shaped by them.

> `Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power…`
> *Hebrews 1:3*

> `And he is before all things, and by him all things consist.`
> *Colossians 1:17*
