The same three-part form turns up wherever one thing is consequential to another: in light and sound, in the copying of DNA, in nerves, in speech, in law and in liturgy. One explanation is coincidence, many different mechanisms happening to share an engineering pattern. This book proposes a deeper one.

If A and B are genuinely related in a consequential sense, something about A must be capable of making a difference to B. That difference must be preserved well enough for B to depend on it. And B must actually be different because of it. That is already T-C-R. On this proposal T-C-R is not a mechanism added to a relational world. It is the operational form of consequential relation itself. It recurs from the substrate to speech because anything consequentially relational must instantiate some version of it.

**Status:** an RS working hypothesis, and one of the book's central ones. It is supported by the recurrence just described and by its economy: one grammar explains why consequence has the same shape across domains that share no mechanism. It would be weakened by a clear case of genuine consequence that cannot be described as a distinction preserved by a dependency, or by a demonstration that the recurrence is better explained as convergent design. Its limits matter as much as its reach. A shared grammar across domains is a structural analogy, not an identity of nature. Light, a gene and a sentence share the form of consequence. They do not thereby become the same kind of thing.

The grammar is also **recursive**. A receiver at one stage is, at once, a source relative to another relation: the molecule in your eye that receives light transmits to the cell, which receives and transmits to the nerve. Consequential relation is therefore not a set of separate pipelines but a network, in which every present state is the reception of earlier distinctions and a source of later ones. This gives a sharper picture of the relation between present actuality and what can happen next, which Chapter 4 raised. Actuality carries its history because past distinctions, received, have become present conditions. They shape what is currently reachable because those present conditions are, in turn, transmitted.

## Cause as consequential relation

The grammar also suggests a precise account of cause and effect, suited to a world in which actualisation is chancy.

In a deterministic picture, a cause *produces* its effect: given the cause, the effect follows. In a stochastic world that cannot be the whole story, because what happens next is open. But a distinction can still make a difference. It can exclude some next states. It can make others possible. It can change how likely they are. It can constrain how events are correlated, preserve an invariant through change, or alter what will be accessible later. Each of these is a way of being causal without producing a fixed result.

The book's working formulation is this:

> **A causal relation exists where a distinction in one relational condition modifies the admissible actualisation, or the consequential state, of another through a distinction-preserving dependency.**

The formulation was checked against the project's simplest relational models before being adopted. In them, a three-way condition changes the likelihood of the next two-way event: a present distinction modifies what happens next by weighting it, without determining it. The initial value of that same condition is soon forgotten: within a short run, nothing in the visible state depends on it any longer. On the formulation, the initial distinction has stopped being causal for that state, because no dependency preserves it, while the condition's *current* value goes on mattering. That is the T-C-R test at work. Rules that forbid a change alter what can be reached at all, and rules that merely favour it alter only how likely it is. Those are two distinct ways of being causal. **Status:** working hypothesis. It fits the models. Whether it is the right account of causation in nature is a question of coherence, not of those models.

The account also disciplines a common word. To say that one change "enabled" another can mean four different things: that it came first (*precedence*); that it removed competitors, so the other became the likelier next event (*competitive clearance*; the project's model reports call this "opportunity", a word this book keeps for the occasion of Chapter 4); that it changed the other's own tendency (*rate*); or that it made the other possible at all (*support*). Only the last two are changes of admissibility or tendency, and only support is the work of a forbidding rule. In the project's later models the senses came apart cleanly. Most soft "enabling" turned out to be competitive clearance.

## Manifestation

There is one further reason T-C-R matters, and it is the deepest. The book has proposed a created relational order beneath the manifest physical world of stones and light. For that order to be manifest at all, as material and experienced reality, there must be a **consequence-preserving relationship** between distinctions in the underlying order and the actual world we meet. If distinctions at the deepest level could make no difference to anything manifest, they would be idle.

That is a minimal claim, and it should be kept minimal. It is tempting to picture something invisible being *transformed* into something visible, as though a hidden object rose through layers and emerged as a stone. That is only one possible architecture, and the book does not assume it. The underlying order and the manifest world might be two descriptions of one relational fact. They might be different resolutions of one order. They might be related by a mapping not yet understood, or in a way not yet conceived. The question of whether the substrate is itself spatial, or whether space arises from it, also remains open. What the book does claim is that, whatever the architecture, consequence must be preserved between them. That is the T-C-R insight applied at its deepest point.

## How T-C-R gathers what came before

T-C-R is not a separate principle added to the previous chapters. It draws them together. It is what mediation requires, if nothing acts across a gap of non-relation (Chapter 3). It is shaped by **admissibility** (Chapter 4) in what a source can transmit, what dependencies exist and what a receiver can register. It is shot through with **constrained chance** (Chapter 5): which molecule in your retina absorbs light from the stone at a given instant is a matter of chance, and the image is steady because many such events compose. And it depends on **identity** (Chapter 6): the carried distinction persists as an equivalence class across changing carriers, with its provenance where something downstream depends on it.

Together these show that a relational world is not a frozen lattice in which everything is related and nothing happens. Relation becomes history: a distinction here makes a difference there, which can in turn be transmitted, carried and received. Life is built from such chains (Chapter 11), and so is human communication (Chapter 12). The theological chapters use the grammar, with care, as a lens on some forms of corruption and restoration (Chapters 14 and 15).

**Status.** Emission, propagation and absorption are established physics, and T-C-R organises that physics without replacing it. It has not been shown to predict anything the physics does not. That T-C-R is the form of consequential relation itself, reaches to the substrate, is recursive and supplies the right account of cause are working hypotheses. Two things are open. In every model the project has built, the dependencies that carry distinctions were designed, and whether created order generates its own carriers from minimal relations is not known. Nor is the architecture of manifestation.

## T-C-R across categories

The same three-part form appears in physics, in biology, in human conversation and in Scripture. Scripture presents God's word as going out and accomplishing its purpose in those who receive it:

> `For as the rain cometh down, and the snow from heaven, and returneth not thither, but watereth the earth, and maketh it bring forth and bud, that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.`
> *Isaiah 55:10-11*

> `How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?… So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.`
> *Romans 10:14, 17*

Isaiah's image is physical (rain that waters the earth), and its subject is God's word that accomplishes his purpose. Paul traces a sequence of sending, preaching, hearing and believing. The form is unmistakably that of something made available, carried and received. In a creation made by the Word, that likeness is not surprising. Chapter 1's four relations say how far it reaches. It is at least a structural analogy. Whether created consequence was also made to represent something of how God's word works is a question about creation's purpose, which Chapter 16 takes up. It is not identity: God's word is not a physical signal, and faith is not the absorption of light. The physical case does not explain the spiritual one, and the spiritual one is not secretly physical.

If anything, the direction of illumination runs the other way. A world made by a God who speaks, and whose word goes out and accomplishes what he purposes, is a world in which it is fitting that even light and sound should be consequential in this way. Physical T-C-R may be one of the ways created order bears the likeness of its Maker.

## The question that remains

Seeing the stone is the reception of one fairly simple distinction. Much of what reaches us is richer: a voice recognised through a wall, a melody heard on a different instrument from the one it was written for, a bird known only from its bones and from drawings by people long dead. These are organised identities, and they survive changes of carrier that might seem bound to destroy them. How they hold together, and how relations become organisations and organisations become new wholes, is the question of Chapter 8.

# Chapter 8: Organised Identity

A cellist draws the bow across the open G string and begins the Prelude of Bach's first Cello Suite: the arpeggiated figure G, D, B, A, B, D, B, D that every cellist knows by heart. Now hear the same opening played on a different cello across town, on a guitar, on a marimba, through a phone's small speaker, from a file of numbers stored on a disc. The wood, the strings, the air, the electronics and the room are all different. In the file there is no sound at all until something plays it. Yet a listener who knows the piece recognises it at once.

Something has persisted across all those changes. It is not a piece of material. Nothing that vibrated in the first cello reaches the phone. It is an organised identity: a pattern of relations among sounds, held together well enough to be recognised. This chapter asks what such identities are, how they survive changes of carrier, and how relations become organisations and organisations become new wholes. Music comes first, because it shows these things with unusual clarity.

## One phrase, many carriers

Begin with what differs between the performances. Each instrument sounds a note as a fundamental frequency together with a series of overtones, and each body shapes those overtones in its own way. That shaping is much of what we call *timbre*, the reason a cello and a guitar sound different on the same note. The rooms add their own reflections. The phone's speaker can scarcely produce the cello's lowest notes at all.

Now consider what survives. A melody is recognised even when it begins on a different note, as when a singer pitches a tune higher or lower. What is preserved then is not any particular frequency but the *relations* between successive pitches, the intervals, which are ratios of frequency. An octave is a ratio of two to one, a perfect fifth very nearly three to two. The four strings of a cello are tuned a fifth apart, C, G, D and A, and the fifth sounds like the same kind of step whether it is played low on the C string or high on the A. Rhythm survives in the same way, as relations among durations, which is why a phrase played a little faster is still the same phrase. Contour, the shape of rising and falling, survives too, and so do harmonic relations.

So the identity of the phrase lives largely in relations among its distinctions, not in the absolute properties of any carrier. That is the first lesson of the chapter, and it is observed, not hypothesised. **The continuity of an organised identity need not depend on the continuity of one particular material carrier.**

## How much can change

Put a loudspeaker badly, tucked into the corner of a room. Sound reflected from the walls meets the sound coming directly from the speaker. At some low frequencies, where the room's dimensions fit whole numbers of half-wavelengths, the reflections reinforce one another into standing waves, and those notes boom. At others they partly cancel, and notes that should be strong almost disappear. The bass line comes out lumpy and uneven. And yet it is still recognisable as the bass line.

Part of the reason lies in the listener. A phone's speaker reproduces almost nothing near 65 cycles a second, the frequency of the cello's lowest C. Yet a listener hears the note at the right pitch, because the ear and brain reconstruct a fundamental from the pattern of its overtones, which the speaker does reproduce. The pitch is recovered from relations among what arrives. This is an identity coherer at work, in the sense of Chapter 7.

There are limits. Change the intervals and the melody becomes a different melody. Scramble the rhythm and the phrase is gone. Distort the sound enough and nothing can recover it. Identity under variation is the equivalence class of Chapter 6 seen from the listener's side: the set of variations that a compatible receiver still treats as the same.

Digital recording makes the receiver's part explicit. Compressed audio formats discard sound that human hearing would not register anyway, such as quiet tones masked by louder ones close in pitch. That is legitimate only relative to a particular receiver. It is the principle of Chapter 6 again: a distinction can safely be dropped only where no reachable consequence draws on it. A measuring microphone, or another species with different hearing, could draw on what was discarded.

Two questions have to be kept apart. One asks whether the identity is preserved in the signal: whether the relations that constitute it are still objectively there. The other asks whether a given receiver can recover it. Interval ratios are in the sound whether or not anyone is listening. Recognising them depends on the receiver's organisation, and listeners differ. A trained musician hears a change of key that an untrained listener misses, and someone with absolute pitch hears the key itself.

## Does the receiver help make the identity?

That raises a harder question. When the ear reconstructs a fundamental the speaker never produced, is the receiver merely recognising an identity that was already complete, or is it taking part in constituting the identity it receives?

The sounds in the room are real whether or not anyone hears them, and the relations among them are objectively there. But the *pitch* heard, a single note at 65 cycles, is not present as a component of the sound. It is what a compatible receiver makes of the relations that are present. A rainbow is a cleaner case still. Sunlight and raindrops are there regardless of any observer. But each observer sees a bow formed by a different set of drops, at an angle fixed by where that observer stands. Two people a few metres apart do not see the same rainbow. Nor does this need consciousness. Strike a chord near a set of tuning forks, and each fork responds to the component that matches its own frequency. Each receives a different identity from the same sound.

Four things are therefore distinct:

- the **source identity**, the distinctions really present at the source;
- the **carried distinctions**, whatever survives the dependency that bears them;
- the **received or reconstructed identity**, what a compatible receiver recovers;
- the **consequential manifestation**, the difference that identity actually makes.

The book's proposal, which the author regards as a credible candidate, is that **a receiver's compatible organisation may be part of what makes a particular identity possible as a consequentially manifested identity**, rather than merely recognising an identity already fully constituted at transmission. This is not the claim that things exist only when perceived. The cello vibrates in an empty hall. Created things are real before anything receives them, as Chapter 1 insisted. Conscious recognition is only one kind of reception. The more basic question is compatible consequential response, and the tuning fork answers to that as truly as the listener. **Status:** RS working hypothesis; its scope is open.

The working principle can now be stated. **A distinguishable identity can remain coherent across changes of instantiation when the relationships necessary for its consequential recognition or operation are preserved through compatible Transmit–Carry–Receive processes.** The book calls this **relational identity compatibility**. It joins Chapter 6's equivalence classes and provenance to Chapter 7's grammar, with the identity organiser and identity coherer as the transmitting and receiving roles it needs.

## Identity without its first carrier

The dodo was a large flightless pigeon of Mauritius, and it was extinct by the end of the seventeenth century. No dodo has lived for more than three hundred years. Yet a good deal is known about it, carried by very different means:

- the accounts of sailors and settlers who saw living birds;
- drawings and paintings, which vary considerably and of which only some were made from live birds;
- bones, many recovered from a marsh in Mauritius;
- the only surviving soft tissue anywhere, a head and a foot kept in Oxford, all that remained of a stuffed bird whose body decayed in the eighteenth century;
- genetic material, which showed in 2002 that the dodo's closest living relative is the Nicobar pigeon of south-east Asia, and from which a whole genome has since been reported, with full publication still awaited.

Each carrier preserves different identity-relevant distinctions, with different fidelity. The paintings preserve impressions of colour and posture, and also the painters' conventions. Studies of the bones have challenged the familiar image of a fat, slow bird, and the bird's exact appearance in life is still debated. The Oxford head carried one distinction for nearly four centuries before anyone could read it. In 2018 detailed scans revealed lead shot in its head and neck: the bird had been shot. The distinction had been carried the whole time. What was new was a compatible receiver.

**The preservation of identity-relevant information is distinguishable from the continued material existence of its original instantiation.** But what is preserved must be kept apart according to what it is about. The dodo as a *species* is a kind, a lineage of populations, and its identity concerns equivalence and descent. The Oxford bird's *historical identity* is that of one individual animal, with its own lineage and provenance. A *reconstruction*, whether a museum model, a computer image or a living bird engineered from a relative to match the genome, would at most fall within a reconstructed equivalence class. It would not be any dodo that lived. Chapter 6 drew the same line between restoring an equivalence class and restoring an individual. Chapter 15 holds the same line for persons: resurrection is God's act, not a reconstruction. And a person is not the information that survives about them.

## History as received distinction

Historical inquiry works this way. An event that no longer occurs leaves distinctions in documents, artefacts, records and testimony. Their usefulness depends on provenance, on fidelity, on compatibility with other evidence, on internal coherence, on corroboration and on preservation against distortion. A historian is a receiver who must judge how much a carrier could have carried and what may have been lost or added along the way. History is a large-scale case of T-C-R across time, and it shows again that coherence is not a method peculiar to physics. The study of the past depends on it entirely.

Charles Darwin was one of the great practitioners of this reasoning, and deserves acknowledgement on his own terms. Much of his argument reconstructed history from preserved distinctions: fossils, the distribution of living things, and shared structures in creatures of very different habits. He attended closely to variation and to the commonality that persists through it, and he knew how limited his carriers were. Following the geologist Charles Lyell, he described the record in the rocks like this:

> For my part, following out Lyell's metaphor, I look at the natural geological record, as a history of the world imperfectly kept, and written in a changing dialect; of this history we possess the last volume alone, relating only to two or three countries. Of this volume, only here and there a short chapter has been preserved; and of each page, only here and there a few lines.
> *Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1859), chapter 9*

That is a careful judgment about what a carrier can preserve. One distinction from his tradition parallels this book's closely. Anatomists, following Richard Owen, distinguished resemblances of underlying structure from resemblances of function, and Darwin read the first kind as evidence of common descent. A shared form is not by itself a shared lineage; lineage needs evidence of provenance. That is the book's own distinction between equivalence and individual continuity, met in natural history. Readers hold different views about the scope of Darwin's theory, and this book does not adjudicate them. Its point concerns method: how history is reconstructed from what survives.

A much later idea borrows Darwin's name. *Quantum Darwinism*, developed by the physicist Wojciech Zurek, proposes that a quantum system leaves many redundant records of certain of its states in its environment, so that observers each reading a small fragment agree about it. The name is a metaphor for states that leave many copies. The theory is physics, not Darwin's work, and its kinship with this chapter is structural: agreement through many independent carriers, as with the dodo (Appendix B).

## From distinction to higher-order identity

Return to the music, and follow it upward. Pressure in the air varies, and a note can be distinguished from silence and from other notes. Those notes stand in relations: intervals, durations, simultaneities. The relations are organised, by harmony and counterpoint, into chords and lines. A major chord, for example, sounds three notes whose frequencies stand close to the ratios four, five and six. And the organisation acquires an identity of its own: this phrase, this movement, this suite. A chord is not an additional material substance, and neither is a melody. Yet each has genuine organisational identity, recognisable across carriers.

The project has long held that something of this shape runs through created order. The first edition arranged it as a ladder of levels, from primitive relation through grouped organisation to things, kinds and higher relational orders; the second edition set the ladder aside as unused. Stated as a process, it is adopted now as a working formulation:

```text
distinction → relationship → organisation → higher-order identity
```

- **Distinction.** Conditions become distinguishable in a way that could matter for some consequence.
- **Relationship.** Distinctions take part in consequential dependencies.
- **Organisation.** Relations form structured configurations under constraint.
- **Higher-order identity.** A configuration acquires recognisable, persistent organisation that can function as a distinguishable whole.

The order is one of articulation, not of priority in being. Chapter 3 holds that relation is foundational, and a distinction is already a relational fact, a difference between conditions. At the lowest order the first two stages may be given together. The grammar marks what each later stage adds.

Not every distinguishable pattern is a new order. Three tests separate a higher-order identity from a pattern that is merely there to be noticed. It must **persist beyond its own constituents**, compared with a matched null, as the project's later models required before anything counted as a reference (Chapter 6). It must be **consequential as a whole**, so that some reachable future responds to it as a unit. And it must be **realisable in more than one way** at the level below, as the phrase is realisable on cello, guitar and disc. These tests absorb the first edition's account of when a whole has crossed "from aggregate to body": shared coupling, disturbance spread through the whole, and properties no single constituent has. **Status:** RS working hypothesis; a working ontological formulation, not a ladder of substances and not a new layer of reality.

## Between orders

The most interesting point is where one order meets the next. A note is itself a higher-order identity: an organisation of vibration that persists, acts as a unit and can be produced on many instruments. In a melody it functions as a single distinction. A phrase, a higher-order identity of notes, functions as a distinction in a movement. So:

```text
higher-order identity at one order → consequential participation in the next
```

How should that step be classified? It might be a fifth stage of the grammar, an interface between orders, the first stage of the next order, or a recursive boundary condition. The book does not settle this. Its working reading is that one identity plays two roles. *Upward*, it is a distinction at the next order. *Downward*, it constrains the relations that sustain it.

Established physics shows the downward role clearly. The physicist Hermann Haken built a general theory of self-organisation, *synergetics*, around the laser. Below a certain power its atoms emit light independently, like a lamp. Above it, one light wave dominates. Its strength, an *order parameter*, is produced by the atoms' emission and then governs that emission, drawing the atoms into step. Haken called this the *slaving principle*, and the loop *circular causality*: the whole arises from the parts and then constrains them. Music has a homely version. A key is established by the notes of a piece, and once established it governs how each later note is heard, as home, as tension, as a step away. Haken's theory is well-tested physics within matter. It does not establish the Relational Substrate, and Haken proposed nothing of the kind. It shows that the downward role is real where it can be observed.

This also clarifies how constraint and consequence relate. A **constraint** affects what may become actual, how states may change, or how likely outcomes are. It confers *potential* consequentiality. A **consequence** occurs when a difference is actually made. The two are closely related and not identical, and T-C-R names the link between them: a constraint becomes consequential when a distinction it governs is received. Identity organisers and coherers can themselves become part of the constraint structure at a higher order, as the key does in music and the order parameter does in a laser.

## One pier at a time

None of this derives gravity, electromagnetism or quantum mechanics from the simplest relational condition, and the book does not ask it to. There may be many orders between the simplest relations and the particles of physics. The author puts the method in an image: we do not need to build a bridge across the Atlantic. We can investigate the construction of one pier and establish what it can support. The project's models are piers of this kind, each an adjacent transition examined exactly, such as the difference between forbidding and favouring (Chapter 4). Negative results are piers too. The hoped-for step from dissolution to new organisation did not appear in the simplest systems (Chapter 9), which shows what that structure will not bear.

One candidate for the transition to material individuality comes from the physics of oscillation. Interacting vibrations can lock their phases, as pendulum clocks on a shared beam fall into step. Coupled modes can trade energy, and cellists know one result as the wolf tone: a note, often near the F or F sharp below middle C, where a string and a strong resonance of the instrument's body couple so tightly that the sound stutters. Nonlinear media can sustain persistent localised patterns: the solitary wave of Chapter 6, and the *oscillons* seen in 1996 in a shaken layer of fine grains, stable peaks that behave like particles and can bind to one another. The question is not whether matter consists of familiar vibrations. It is whether interacting activity can produce persistent, consequential distinctions, and whether identity might reside in *relations among modes*, as a melody's resides in its intervals. The first edition spoke of phase and coupling, and the technical volume's knotted structures remain candidates. **Status:** mechanism candidate. Oscillation is not assumed to be a primitive of the substrate. It is a candidate the author favours, and in a second role as well: as an intrinsic reference cadence by which succession in created order could be compared and measured (Chapter 6). The two roles are separate, and neither makes oscillation the source of succession.

Music shows that higher-order identity emerges within matter. It does not show how matter emerges, and the beauty of the analogy is no reason to blur the two (Chapter 6). Nor is a soul a melody played on a body: persons, as Chapter 12 will show, are a category of their own.

## The question that remains

Identities, then, can be organised, carried across changes of instantiation, recovered by compatible receivers and gathered into higher orders. All of this rests on something the chapter has assumed rather than explained. The light from the stone reaches your eye as a vast number of individual events, each a matter of chance, and yet you see a steady image. A melody survives a badly placed loudspeaker because many small chance processes add up to reliable sound. If what happens at the deepest level is constrained chance, where does such exact regularity come from? And what is the mathematics that describes it so well? Those are the questions of Chapter 9.

# Chapter 9: Regularity, Coordination, and the Place of Mathematics

Pump up a bicycle tyre and feel it grow firm. The pressure you feel is the combined effect of a vast number of air molecules striking the inner wall. Each moves erratically, its path impossible to follow. Yet the pressure is steady, and it obeys a simple law: squeeze the air into half the volume at the same temperature and the pressure doubles. Out of the tumult of individual molecules comes a regularity you can write in a single line.

The previous chapters proposed that what happens at the deepest level of created order is constrained chance, and that distinctions reach us through chains of transmission, each made of many chancy events. This chapter asks how such a world can be so reliably regular. Light bends through a lens by exactly the amount the optician calculates. The stone is the same weight tomorrow. And the chapter asks what mathematics, which describes this regularity so well, is in relation to the world it describes.

Several different problems are hidden inside the question of regularity, and it helps to separate them at the start. First, events described probabilistically can combine into stable aggregates without settling whether the underlying processes are themselves chancy. Second, the way those events are related to one another can change the behaviour of the whole, even when the chance of each event stays exactly the same. Third, a simple mathematical law can describe the whole accurately at one scale without describing what happens beneath it. And fourth, such a description may leave out lower-level distinctions that do not matter for the question it answers but do matter for others. These are different problems. The chapter takes them in turn, and the examples that follow (coins, rings, fluids and hidden structure) each belong to one of them.

## Regularity from many chances

Part of the answer has long been understood, and it belongs to mainstream science rather than to the Relational Substrate project. When very many events are described statistically, their aggregate can be highly predictable even when individual outcomes are uncertain to us. Flip a coin ten times and you might get seven heads. Flip it ten million times and the proportion of heads will almost certainly lie within a tenth of a per cent of a half. This is the **law of large numbers**. In its simplest familiar form it concerns independent events. Mathematicians have proved versions of it for events that are dependent on one another, provided the dependence fades enough over time or distance.

Physics uses statistical regularities in many places: the gas laws; the jittering of small particles in water, which Albert Einstein traced in 1905 to the irregular impacts of molecules; and the precise half-lives of Chapter 5. These observations establish reliable aggregate behaviour, not by themselves a fundamentally stochastic microscopic ontology. Classical statistical mechanics can use deterministic underlying dynamics; quantum decay is predicted probabilistically, while its ontological interpretation remains contested.

Physicists call such laws **effective**: they hold to great precision at the scale where they apply, without describing what happens underneath. The book uses the phrase **effective determinism** for behaviour that is regular, reliable and predictable to the precision we can observe, whatever the underlying process. It is a fact about regularity, not a metaphysical claim that nothing could have happened otherwise.

Two neighbouring ideas need to be kept apart from it. **Mathematical determinism** is a property of equations: given the state at one moment, the equations fix the state at every later moment. Many of the equations of physics are deterministic in this sense, including the fluid equations discussed below, even when they describe aggregates through effective variables. A deterministic large-scale description does not decide whether the underlying processes are themselves deterministic or ontologically stochastic. And an **attractor** is a precisely defined idea in the mathematics of changing systems. It is a state, or set of states, toward which a system tends from a wide range of starting points and to which it returns when slightly disturbed. The word is easily used loosely for any outcome that turns up often. But a reliable outcome is not by itself evidence of an attractor: the illustration in Chapter 5 reached the right answer every time because of conservation, not because anything drew it there.

## Same odds, different behaviour

Averaging answers the first problem: many microscopic events can produce nearly steady tyre pressure, whether their underlying dynamics are deterministic or stochastic. But an average is only one feature of a whole. The second problem begins with a simple puzzle.

Imagine two rooms, each with a hundred people tossing fair coins at the same moment, again and again. In the first room everyone tosses independently. In the second, people are paired, and each pair agrees in advance that whatever one gets, the partner will report the opposite. For any single person, in either room, the chance of heads is exactly one half. Nothing about the individual odds differs. Yet the rooms behave completely differently as wholes. In the first room the number of heads wanders from toss to toss, sometimes 44, sometimes 57. In the second room it is exactly fifty, every time.

The individual chances, what statisticians call the **marginal** probabilities, are identical. What differs is how the events are related to one another: the **joint process**. Two systems can assign exactly the same probability to every individual event and still behave quite differently as wholes, because in one the events are tied together and in the other they are not. In short:

```text
the same individual odds
  are not the same joint process,
  which is not the same pattern of co-variation,
  which is not the same behaviour of the whole
```

## Coordination that matters

The book calls such relations among chance events **coordination**, and the word needs care in two directions.

First, coordination does not mean a controller standing over the events and arranging them. In the second room nobody directs the tosses. The coordination lies in the fact that each pair acts as one. Coordination is a relation among events, not an agent above them.

Second, and more important, coordination is not what makes an average stable. Ordinary aggregation already does that, as the tyre showed. Coordination matters for the other features of a whole, the ones that individual chances do not fix:

- how large the fluctuations are, and what shape they take;
- whether a quantity is held *exactly*, not merely on average;
- how the whole moves from moment to moment along its path;
- how it responds when disturbed;
- which future states remain open to it.

The two rooms of coin-tossers had the same average. They differed in everything else.

Exploratory work on rings of locally coupled chance events, not yet a formal record, sharpens the point. Units with the same local chances produced very different global behaviour depending on how their fluctuations were coupled. Correlation as such was not what mattered: a strong dependence can be irrelevant to a property, and a modest one decisive if it is aligned with what matters. Coordination that tightens where a fluctuation would do harm behaves differently from coordination applied uniformly. Stability also comes in layers. A whole can be stable in its mean while its fluctuations are not, and some quantities can be exactly conserved while others still vary.

None of this mathematics belongs to a relation-first ontology. Probability theory, statistical mechanics and network science describe dependence and coupling with great sophistication, and object-based models represent them routinely. What the relational proposal changes is the reading. On an object-first reading, the dependence structure is an extra fact about how already-complete things happen to be related. On the relational reading, it belongs to *what the physical whole is*: the coordination of its parts is part of their constitution, not a statistic laid over them. That is the book's ontological proposal about the mathematics, not a discovery within it. Nor does the book claim that local relations alone account for the regularity of created order as a whole. Its claim is that the regularity is real, and that local relation, coordination and constraint are part of how it holds.

## What mathematics is doing

The regularities of the physical world are described by mathematics, often with astonishing success. In 1960 the physicist Eugene Wigner wrote of "the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences": structures worked out by mathematicians for their own sake turn out, again and again, to describe nature with precision nobody expected. What is the mathematics doing?

Consider the equations that describe moving fluids, such as air over a wing or water in a pipe. They are called the Navier–Stokes equations, after two nineteenth-century scientists, and they are used every day to design aircraft and forecast weather. They treat a fluid as a smooth, continuous substance. Yet a fluid is made of molecules in constant chaotic motion. The equations work because, at the scale where engineers use them, the molecules' combined behaviour is regular enough to be described *as if* the fluid were smooth, and physicists can derive the equations approximately from that statistical behaviour. In very thin gases the smooth description fails and the molecular picture takes over. Whether the equations always have smooth solutions is still one of the great unsolved problems of mathematics.

This shows two things. First, deterministic mathematics at one scale does not imply that reality is deterministic at every scale. Second, a smooth field description need not be the ontology of what it describes. Water is not made of the continuous field the equations describe, and the equations are still true at their scale.

The Relational Substrate project takes from this a research question rather than a result. The question it asks is this: *what kinds of relational constraint and coordination preserve the right invariants, correlations and continuity for stable effective laws to emerge at all?* That is a real question, because, as the coin rooms showed, not every arrangement of chance produces stable laws. It is also an open one.

## Hidden structure beneath a description

There is a further caution, connected to Chapter 6. A description can map many different underlying states onto one visible picture, and the hidden differences can still shape what happens next.

The project's simplest relational models give a striking, exact instance. Add a genuinely three-way relation among three points, a link joining all three at once that can exist independently of the ordinary two-way links, and ask what an observer who sees only the two-way links would find. Wherever the three-way relation could influence the two-way ones, the next visible change depended not only on how the visible links were now but on how they had just been. The visible process *appeared to have memory*, although nothing in the rules recorded the past. The memory was produced by hiding a present relation. A coarse description can turn hidden present structure into what looks like history.

So **mathematical equivalence under one description does not settle whether two things are the same.** A coarse description is often exactly right for its purpose. But whether what it leaves out is truly irrelevant depends on whether any reachable future process draws on it. That is the same principle Chapter 6 applied to identity, now applied to the mathematics of regularity.

The general lesson is the one Chapter 2 drew, now sharpened. **A mathematical structure that successfully describes behaviour is not, by that fact, the thing that reality fundamentally is.** Mathematics describes regularities, stable relations, invariants and the aggregate behaviour of coordinated processes, and it describes them so well because they are genuinely there. That is a reason for great respect toward mathematics, owed to what it captures, without confusing the description with the described.

On the relational proposal, mathematics works because created order is structured by constraint, preserved by equivalence and invariance, and regular in aggregate through coordination. Those are precisely the things mathematics is best at describing. Scripture speaks of the heavens in exactly this register of ordered disclosure:

> `The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork. Day unto day uttereth speech, and night unto night sheweth knowledge. There is no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard.`
> *Psalm 19:1-3*

> `Knowest thou the ordinances of heaven? canst thou set the dominion thereof in the earth?`
> *Job 38:33*

> `For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead.`
> *Romans 1:20*

Creation is intelligible: it can be "understood by the things that are made". Its ordinances can be known, though not commanded. This is the ground of science, and it is why science can be trusted within its domain. Scripture does not tell us the Navier–Stokes equations. It tells us why a world in which such equations hold, and in which human minds can find them, is exactly what one should expect of a creation made through the Word.

## Measurement, model and interpretation

The layers of Chapter 2 apply here with full force. What physics measures about gravity, light and magnetism, and what its mathematics predicts, constrain every ontology, this one included. Electromagnetism, from Maxwell's equations to quantum electrodynamics, predicts with precision unmatched in any other field of knowledge. Where established measurement and prediction stand, they stand, and the relational reading must agree with them.

What a field is, whether spacetime is a thing or an ordering of relations, whether quantum chance is fundamental, and what a particle is between measurements are questions of interpretation, and they remain open. The equations do not dictate the answers. When an answer is presented as though they did, a metaphysical assumption has borrowed the authority of a measurement. The remedy is not to distrust measurement. It is to notice the assumption, and to test it for coherence like any other proposal.

Quantum field theory, the framework in which the particles of physics are described, needs particular care, because it is where the slide from description to ontology is easiest. Five things are distinct here: the mathematical formalism, which assigns mathematical objects to the points of spacetime; the measurable phenomena it predicts so superbly, such as scattering rates and spectral lines; interpretations of what its states and operators represent; the claim that fields are the fundamental realities; and the claim that whatever is fundamental is material. The success of the mathematics bears directly on the second. It does not by itself establish the third, fourth or fifth. Chapter 6 noted that the same mathematics of quantised excitations describes vibrations in a crystal, where nobody concludes that a new material entity exists. That does not show that electrons are like crystal vibrations. It shows that the formalism alone does not decide. Equally, nothing in the formalism proves the relational substrate. What the book asks is compatibility: whatever the substrate is, it must yield what the formalism predicts.

## Gravity and time in the simplest models

Chapter 2 opened with a question the book has not answered: what *is* gravity? The project does not know. Its Gravity/Time programme asked something narrower, and its answers are exact results on systems of at most seven points, adopted at that scope (Appendix E.8).

A rule that favours some pattern of links defines a *relational potential*: a count of that pattern, weighted by the rule. The system spends more time where the count is high. "Attraction" toward a structure is then participation in the favoured pattern, with no named centre and no force reaching across. **Status:** mechanism candidate, in models only. **Gathering**, a lasting preference for relation to a reference structure, is not **succession** (Chapter 6). As the models grew from six points to seven, the directed handover kept its direction in every case, while the only gathering seen alongside it fell to the level of the comparison. Much apparent gathering is density alone, so a claim of gathering must survive adjustment for density. And a reference made of relations is not a neutral frame: its own links take part through the same rules.

There is also a negative result. The rules do *not* tie the rate of activity to the potential: the same preferred states admit very different rates near a structure and far from it. Measured clocks really do run slower deeper in a gravitational field, so a relational reading of that fact would need a principle these rules do not contain. Every model claim about attraction or time must also name its clock, because counting steps and measuring continuous time can give opposite answers. None of this is gravity, and none of it is a theory of time.

## What would count against these proposals

A proposal that cannot be wrong in any identifiable way tells us little. So it is worth stating what would count against the specific claims of Chapters 3 to 8, and where they are currently hard to test.

- **Contradicting precise measurement.** Any specific Relational Substrate mechanism that contradicted a precise measurement would fail, however coherent it looked. This has already happened. A model the project built in 2026 predicted the direction of an effect in metal fatigue but its size many times too small, and the project recorded it as a failure of magnitude rather than adjusting the model to fit.
- **Intrinsic properties at the base.** The relation-first proposal (Chapter 3) would be seriously weakened if physics came to show that its most fundamental entities have fully intrinsic properties, fixed independently of every interaction. The trend of the last century runs the other way, but the question is open.
- **Entanglement and mediation.** The proposal that influence is always mediated (Chapters 3 and 7) faces real pressure from quantum entanglement. Measurements on two distant entangled particles show correlations that, by Bell's theorem, no theory satisfying certain locality assumptions can reproduce, and experiments have confirmed those correlations. They cannot be used to send a signal, which is why relativity is not violated, and several interpretations, including relational ones, give accounts of them. Bell's theorem rules out a specific class of local explanations, not every conceivable notion of mediation. But entanglement remains the hardest test case for an account of mediated relation, and it is not a solved problem for this one.
- **Gravity's clocks.** The project has no relational account of gravitational time dilation, and its simplest models show that one would need a principle they do not contain (above). That is an open gap, not yet a refutation, and it marks where a relational account of gravity is most exposed.
- **The stochastic hypothesis is currently hard to test.** The standard interpretations of quantum theory agree on every measurement made so far, so present evidence cannot decide between a fundamentally chancy world and a deterministic one at that level. (Theories that modify quantum dynamics with spontaneous collapse do make slightly different predictions, which experiments are now testing.) That protects the hypothesis from easy refutation, and it is also a reason to hold it no more firmly than a coherent hypothesis.
- **Matter's emergence stays unexplained.** Proposition B (Chapter 3) owes an account of how stable material individuals arise within an order that is not itself material. Its mechanism would be weakened if investigation of adjacent transitions (Chapter 8) kept failing to produce persistent, individuated organisation from simpler relations. The book's independent, comparative argument for B would be weakened if Proposition A or C came to explain universal interoperability with equal economy; the author's theological premise of a non-material origin rests on other grounds. At present the debt is unpaid, not defaulted.
- **The models do not single out RS.** The project's models demonstrate possibilities. Ordinary computer science and probability account for every result they produced. The laboratory's most recent generation also recorded a negative result: a pattern of "dissolution leading to new organisation" that the project hoped to find in its simplest systems did not appear (Appendix B). Results of this kind narrow what the ideas can claim. They show that the ideas are coherent and workable, not that nature uses them.

These limits do not empty the proposals of value. They locate it. The value lies in coherence: in whether a relation-first account of physical order, with constrained chance, relational identity and consequential transmission, helps the whole of what we know hang together better than its alternatives. That is the test to which the next chapter turns.

## From the stone to everything else

The physical arc of the book is now complete. The stone is a stable, history-bearing configuration within a created order of relation, seen through a chain of preserved dependency, and regular enough to be written in exact mathematics because many constrained and coordinated chance events add up to a reliable whole.

The problem underneath this whole chapter, then, is not merely how randomness averages out. Mainstream science already understands that well. It is what relational organisation makes stable identity, stable consequence and stable effective law possible across scales, while preserving the distinctions that still matter. Averaging, coordination, effective equations and hidden structure are four different parts of that one question. The Relational Substrate project has learned to ask it more precisely.

So far this is an account of stones and light. The book's claim, however, is that it matters for far more than stones and light, and that a relation-first physical world changes how the rest of reality, including you, can be understood. Chapter 10 makes that case.

# Chapter 10: Why Relation Matters Beyond Physics

On Monday you promise a friend that you will help her move house on Saturday. On Saturday morning you would rather stay in bed. You get up and go.

It is an ordinary scene, as ordinary as the stone on the path, and like the stone it rests on a great deal. For the promise to be what it seems, several things must be true. The person who gets up on Saturday must be the same person who spoke on Monday, though much in you has changed in between. Your words on Monday must have gone out from you and become something in her: an expectation, a plan, a reliance she has built on. What you do on Saturday must have consequences for her, and through her for others. And there must be something about the promise that *binds* you. It is not merely that you predicted you would go, but that you *owe* it. If you had stayed in bed, she would have been wronged, not merely surprised.

Identity through time, a distinction carried from one person to another and received as a change in her, consequence, obligation, belonging: these are among the most basic features of human life. This chapter asks how they sit with what the physical world fundamentally is. That is the question the earlier chapters have been preparing, and it is the hinge of the book.

## The tests the answer must pass

Chapter 2 distinguished local, regional and global coherence. It also argued that global coherence asks more than the absence of contradiction. The domains of an account must be genuinely connected. Ideas must cross from one domain to another without silently changing kind. Claims must keep their meaning through the layers. A claim taken round a cycle of domains must return the same. And the real distinctions must survive all of this.

The promise is a good place to apply those tests, because it crosses every boundary the book cares about. It involves a body that walks to a friend's house: physics and biology. It involves a person who remembers and intends: personal life. It involves an obligation: moral order. And for a Christian it involves faithfulness before God. A picture of the physical world must not only explain falling stones. It must allow the transitions from stone to body to person to promise to be intelligible, without contradiction and without reducing any of them to another.

## The serious alternatives

It would be easy to set up the question as a contest between the relational picture and a crude alternative: a world of hard, self-contained lumps, each with properties entirely its own, that only bump into one another. Some philosophers have held views close to that. A well-known modern version holds that the world is a vast mosaic of local, intrinsic facts, with everything else, including causes and laws, supervening on how those facts happen to be arranged. That view deserves a hearing. But it is not the strongest alternative, and an argument aimed only at it would prove little.

The serious alternatives already contain a great deal of relation.

- **Powers ontologies** hold that the basic properties of things are dispositions to act on, and be acted on by, other things. A power is already directed beyond its bearer.
- **Field ontologies,** which many physicists hold, treat fields spread through all of space as the basic physical reality, so that particles are disturbances in something continuous and everywhere interacting.
- **Hylomorphic accounts,** in the tradition of Aristotle and Aquinas, hold that things are constituted by form, and that form is intrinsically ordered toward activity and toward other things.
- **Process philosophies** take events and their connections to be more basic than enduring substances.
- **Structural realism** holds that what our best theories most securely describe is structure, the pattern of relations.

These are serious positions held by serious people. Several of them converge, in important ways, with the view this book defends. The question is therefore not whether the alternatives can make room for relation. Many of them can. It is *where* relation enters, and what that costs. Chapter 3 named one cost every ontology must meet: independently located things everywhere share one grammar of interaction. Where an alternative supplies that common interface through a field, a law, a form or a set of powers, the fair question is what work that common structure is doing, and whether it is constitutive relation under another name.

## Where relation enters

Here is the difference that matters. In the relational picture this book proposes, relation is *constitutive* at the base. What a physical thing is cannot be specified apart from how it stands to others. Chapter 6 even defined the identity of a thing by what could distinguish it in relation to possible future interactions. The contrast that matters is with ontologies in which the fundamental entities are individuated wholly or substantially independently of constitutive relation, so that what a thing is can be fully specified before its relations are. In such ontologies relation is something already-complete bearers *have*, *exercise* or *enter into*. It is not what they *are*. Not every substance ontology is like this. A sophisticated powers theorist may hold that a thing's essential powers are other-directed from the start, and a hylomorphist may hold that form and its ordered capacities are constitutive from the beginning. Those views already share part of what this book defends, and the argument below is not aimed at them.

That difference may look slight in physics, where both kinds of ontology describe the falling stone equally well. It becomes significant when the account must cross into human life, because human life is pervaded by relation that is not merely exercised but constitutive. You are, in part, *who you are* through your parents, your promises, your friendships, your history with others and your standing before God. A person is not a self-contained individual who then enters relationships, as a billiard ball enters collisions. Personal identity is relational in a much stronger sense.

So an ontology whose fundamental entities are individuated independently of constitutive relation must, at some point on the way from stones to persons, introduce constitutive relation as something new: a kind of reality that its base does not contain in any form. That is not impossible. But it is a discontinuity. It adds a bridge assumption that has to be explained, or accepted without explanation, somewhere between physics and personhood.

A relation-first ontology does not need that bridge. Its base already has the *form* of what appears, transformed and deepened, in human life:

- constitutive relation (Chapter 3);
- identity as relational equivalence carrying its own history (Chapter 6);
- distinctions preserved by dependency and received as consequence (Chapter 7);
- wholes stabilised by the coordination of their parts (Chapter 9).

When relation becomes personal and moral, it does not appear as a stranger from a different reality. It appears in a world whose grain it already follows.

## The argument, stated plainly

The central argument of the book can now be stated in steps:

1. Human life, as we live it and as Scripture describes it, is pervaded by constitutive relation, identity through change, consequence that passes from one person to another, and responsibility.
2. A physical ontology whose fundamental entities are individuated independently of constitutive relation must introduce constitutive relationality for the first time at some higher level, as a new kind of reality.
3. A physical ontology in which relation is constitutive at the base already contains the form of these features, so that living, personal and moral relation are continuous in form with the physical order they arise in, while remaining distinct in kind.
4. Other things being equal, an account with fewer unexplained discontinuities and fewer ad hoc bridge assumptions between its domains is more globally coherent, by the tests of connection and faithful translation.
5. Therefore, *if* a relation-first picture of physical order is consistent with everything we observe, it is to be preferred on grounds of global coherence.

The argument does not claim that other ontologies make promises impossible or responsibility unintelligible. That would be stronger than the book needs, and probably false. It claims something more modest and more defensible: relation-first ontology offers a more *economical continuity of form* across physical, living and personal reality, provided the boundaries between categories stay intact. The conditional in step 5 matters. That is why Chapters 3 to 9 took such care over what physics does and does not say.

If the argument is sound, it shows why the physics of this book is not an optional technical appendix to a theological book. *How* the material world is real bears on whether the rest of reality hangs together.

## Continuity, not reduction

The common relational grounding of material things is a kind of glue. It allows physical causation, biological organisation, embodied action, consequence in the environment, communication and social dependence to belong to one created order. But it is continuity across the boundaries, not reduction across them:

- Moral obligation is not a field, and a promise is not a force.
- Love is not covariance.
- Sin is not entropy.
- The soul is not a carrier.
- Resurrection is not the substrate repairing itself.
- Divine action is not a wider set of physical permissions.

The relational picture does not tell you that you ought to keep your promise. Chapter 13 will distinguish what is physically possible from what is morally right, and insist that the first never settles the second. What the relational picture does is remove the strangeness of a world in which promises could bind at all.

## The strongest objection: emergence

The most serious reply runs like this. Nobody claims that promises exist among particles. They *emerge*. Complex arrangements display properties their parts lack: wetness emerges from molecules that are not wet, and life from chemistry that is not alive. Why should constitutive relation not emerge in the same way, from a base without it?

The book accepts emergence fully. Chapter 11 will argue that living organisation is genuinely new and genuinely explanatory at its own level. The disagreement is narrower. In familiar cases, what emerges is a new and higher expression of capacities the base already has. Wetness expresses the attraction molecules already have for one another. Life expresses chemistry that already includes catalysis, templating and self-assembly. The question is not whether new properties appear. It is whether the base already contains the *relational resources* that make the emergent structures intelligible.

If the base contains entities individuated independently of their relations, whose relations are always something added or exercised, then constitutive relation emerges from a base where nothing is constituted by its relations. That can be asserted, but it is precisely the kind of discontinuity step 2 names. A powers ontology narrows the gap, because powers are already other-directed, and the book counts that as convergence. It does not count it as refutation. The relational picture's claim is a claim of *continuity of structural capacity*: what emerges in living, personal and moral life is new in kind, and it emerges from a base that already has its form. It is not a claim to derive moral truth from physics. That is a more coherent position, and its warrant is comparative: it rests on global coherence.

## A second case: the poisoned river

A factory upstream discharges waste into a river. Downstream, fish die, and the people of a village who drink the water fall ill. Each link is physical: chemicals are released, carried in the water, and received as changes in the bodies of fish and people, a chain of transmissions crossing from chemistry to biology to human life. But the case is also moral. Someone is responsible, and the villagers have been wronged.

Apply the round-trip test. Begin with the physical chain, translate it into the moral question of responsibility, then into the action required (stop the discharge, compensate the village), and back into the physical world (cleaner water). In a relational creation, every step of that cycle concerns the same world. Responsibility answers to *real* consequences flowing through a *real* order of relation, and the remedy flows back through the same order. The moral layer is distinct, since responsibility is not a chemical fact. But it is not a separate story attached from outside.

Scripture speaks of exactly this reach, in which human wrongdoing is received by the land itself:

> `Hear the word of the LORD, ye children of Israel: for the LORD hath a controversy with the inhabitants of the land, because there is no truth, nor mercy, nor knowledge of God in the land. By swearing, and lying, and killing, and stealing, and committing adultery, they break out, and blood toucheth blood. Therefore shall the land mourn, and every one that dwelleth therein shall languish, with the beasts of the field, and with the fowls of heaven; yea, the fishes of the sea also shall be taken away.`
> *Hosea 4:1-3*

> `For the earnest expectation of the creature waiteth for the manifestation of the sons of God. For the creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who hath subjected the same in hope… For we know that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now.`
> *Romans 8:19-20, 22*

Hosea's land mourns because of the people's lying and killing. Paul's whole creation groans. Scripture consistently presents human moral life and the created world as bound together, so that wrong done by persons is received in the land, and the redemption of persons concerns the whole creation. The book does not claim that a relational physics *explains* these texts. Their explanation is theological. The claim is that a relational account of the material world sits naturally with the world they describe, while an account of sealed and indifferent objects makes them sound like poetry about a reality that is not really like that.

The author goes further. On the author's account the created order is designed to bear moral consequence: it is the theatre in which embodied persons act and the language in which their acts take effect, are carried and are answered. **Status:** theological premise about creation's purpose. It is not derived from the physics. It names what the physics, on the relational reading, is fitted to serve.

## Why this is a Christian question

This argument bears on Christian faith in a particular way.

Scripture describes a world in which relation is fundamental at every level. God makes humanity in his image and declares that it is not good for the man to be alone (Genesis 2:18). He binds himself to his people by covenant. He calls them to love, to keep faith and to bear one another's burdens. In Christ he reconciles "all things unto himself… whether they be things in earth, or things in heaven" (Colossians 1:20). If the physical world were, at bottom, a world in which nothing is constituted by its relations, this scriptural world would rest on a creation of a different kind, and the transition would need explaining. If the physical world is relational from its foundation, created by the God in whom "all things consist", then the relational life Scripture describes is the fulfilment, at its own level, of the grain of the whole creation. That does not prove the gospel. It removes one reason for thinking the gospel must be about a world other than the one we physically inhabit.

## Coherence, error and convergence

Chapter 2 said that coherence is not truth. The danger has a subtler form: an argument can become *more* coherent as it proceeds while moving *further* from the truth, if every step builds on an early mistake nobody questions. The research behind this project met this directly, though in exploratory work rather than in formally recorded experiments. While developing an AI-assisted method of reasoning that runs several independent lines of thought on one problem, the author observed that when the lines were repeatedly merged into a shared summary and fed back, agreement rose steadily, and an error present in one early line could harden into a confident consensus. The project calls this a *false attractor*. The lesson, which this book adopts, is that coherence is not the same as fidelity to the truth. Agreement can be produced by a shared hidden premise as easily as by a shared grasp of reality.

The remedy is to ask where agreement came from. When lines of inquiry that are genuinely independent, starting from different premises, drawing on different evidence and reasoning by different routes, arrive at relationships that fit together, their agreement carries weight no single line could. The book calls this **independent relational convergence**. The dodo of Chapter 8 is an example: sailors' accounts, bones, a preserved head and a genome, each with its own provenance, constrain the same bird. Its strength depends on the independence being real. Many voices repeating one source are one source. Several AI systems trained on overlapping material and fed one another's summaries are not independent witnesses merely because they are separate programs, which is how the false attractor formed.

Error has its own anatomy, and it tells more than a verdict of "false". Take 2 + 2 = 5. Almost everything in it is sound. The numbers mean what they always mean. Addition is a well-defined operation. The question, what two and two make, has a definite answer, and five is an intelligible candidate. The error lies in one place: the asserted relation between the operation and its result. A statement that could not be understood could not even be wrong, so intelligible error depends on genuine coherence. That does not mean every falsehood hides a true conclusion, or that a false relation becomes true because its surroundings are intelligible. It means that when a claim fails, the right response is to find the relationship that failed, keep what remains sound, and notice what the failure has excluded. A failed hypothesis can correct the question as well as the answer. Stories show the same separation from the other side. A novel can be coherent throughout and never have happened: whether an account holds together, and whether it reports what occurred, are two questions.

This is not an account of moral evil, which Chapter 14 gives. A mistaken representation is an error of relation. Wrongdoing is a person's turning against the good. They can coincide, but one is not the other.

All this applies to the book itself. Its own coherence could be a false attractor. The safeguards are those already described. The argument stays accountable to observation wherever observation can reach (Chapter 9 named where it cannot). It keeps its levels of claim distinct. It keeps alternatives in view (Appendix A). And it submits its conclusions to Scripture, which is not one more input to the coherence but the frame within which coherence is sought.

There is also a reason this matters for global coherence in particular. Global coherence is the most demanding test there is, because it must hold across every domain at once, and because errors hidden in one domain tend to surface as drift on the round trip through the others. A false attractor in one place is likely, sooner or later, to produce a contradiction or a silent change of meaning somewhere else. That is exactly why global coherence is a stronger test than local success, and why the book is willing to be judged by it.

## Relation across categories

![Figure 5. Relation across categories. Material, living, personal, moral and spiritual realities are distinct kinds, not layers built one out of another; relation runs through each in its own way; God is not a category within creation but its Creator, who upholds all things.](v2/figures/fig-categories.png)

The chapter can now complete what Chapter 1 began. Creation contains distinct categories of reality, and relation appears in each of them differently.

- In the **physical** world, relation is constraint, equivalence, coordination and the carriage of distinctions (Chapters 3 to 9).
- In the **living** world, it becomes metabolism, signalling, templating and repair (Chapter 11).
- In the **personal** world, it becomes address and response, knowledge and love, promise and trust (Chapter 12).
- In the **moral** world, it becomes obligation, rightness and wrong (Chapter 13).
- In the **spiritual** world, it becomes communion with God.
- God's relation to creation is that of Creator to creature. It belongs to no category within creation, and every created relation depends on it.

The same word, *relation*, is used across all these categories, and it is used truly. What runs through them is a continuity of form, not a single nature. The remaining chapters take the categories one at a time, beginning with life, and show how each stands within a relational creation without being swallowed by it.

# Chapter 11: Life

Turn the stone over. Underneath, in the damp, there is a woodlouse, a pale root, a thread of fungus, perhaps a small seed beginning to split. A moment ago the book was concerned with a lump of mineral. Now it faces things that feed, grow, respond, repair themselves and make more of their own kind.

Life is one of the clearest realities in the world, and one of the hardest for any account of reality to place well. Some pictures of the world are confident as long as they deal with inert matter and become hesitant once life appears in earnest. If the relational account is right, life should not need a separate explanatory afterthought. Nor should it be flattened into chemistry that merely happens to be complicated. This chapter asks what life is, within a relational creation, and where Scripture draws its boundaries.

## Life is given

Scripture places life near the centre of creation, and it speaks of it in a particular way. Life is commanded and ordered:

> `And God said, Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind, cattle, and creeping thing, and beast of the earth after his kind: and it was so.`
> *Genesis 1:24*

And life is given, held and sustained by God, not possessed by living things in their own right:

> `The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life.`
> *Job 33:4*

> `Thou hidest thy face, they are troubled: thou takest away their breath, they die, and return to their dust. Thou sendest forth thy spirit, they are created: and thou renewest the face of the earth.`
> *Psalm 104:29-30*

> `Neither is worshipped with men's hands, as though he needed any thing, seeing he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things.`
> *Acts 17:25*

The pattern is consistent. Living things are real, active and their own: Genesis says the earth *brings forth* them, and they bring forth after their kind. Yet their life is never self-grounding. It is given, upheld and, in the end, withdrawn by God. The book holds both together. The account of living organisation that follows describes how life operates within created order. It does not describe where life ultimately comes from, which Scripture locates in the gift of God.

## Life as sustained organisation

What distinguishes the woodlouse from the stone? Both are configurations within created order, and both persist. The difference lies in *how* they persist.

The stone persists largely by being left alone: its crystal structure is stable, and the changes it ordinarily undergoes do not disturb it. A living thing persists in the opposite way. It is constantly taking in matter and energy, transforming them, and expelling what it no longer needs. A woodlouse is not a fixed collection of molecules. It is a pattern of organisation that keeps re-establishing itself through a continuous flow of material, like the flame of Chapter 6, but enormously more intricate and active. It maintains itself, repairs damage, responds to its surroundings, grows according to a characteristic pattern and reproduces.

So life is **sustained organisation**: persistence that is actively maintained, under many layers of constraint, by the continual work of the living thing itself. In the terms of Chapter 6, a living thing maintains its organised continuity by continually *re-actualising* itself within its relevant equivalence class, where the stone keeps its own largely by being undisturbed, and by actively correcting departures from it. Its continuing individuality also depends on the unbroken history of that living process. A living thing does not merely persist. It works to stay what it is.

## Signals within signals

Much of that activity is transmission. When a cell detects food, a hormone or a threat, a molecule at its surface changes shape. That change is released into a chain of further molecular changes, carried through the cell, and received at its destination as a determinate change: a gene switched on, a movement begun, a substance secreted. One cell signals to another by releasing molecules that are carried through the fluid between them and received at the other's surface. Nerves carry impulses, as Chapter 7 described. Hormones carry differences through the bloodstream from one organ to another.

A living body is, among other things, a vast composition of transmissions, nested within one another and running in parallel and in sequence. They are coordinated so that the whole responds as one. The grammar of Chapter 7, transmit, carry, receive (T-C-R), applies here with full force, and it applies more richly than it did to the stone and the light.
